swin.lead: Swin gave back to the Vision Transformer the two properties ViT had discarded — locality and a resolution pyramid — without abandoning attention. Self-attention is computed inside small fixed windows, so cost grows linearly rather than quadratically in pixel count, and alternating blocks shift the window grid so information still crosses window boundaries. It is what made a Transformer usable as a general detection and segmentation backbone rather than a classifier.

blocks.h: Why ViT could not do detection
blocks.b:
ViT emits a single sequence of $16\times16$ patches at one scale and keeps it at that scale through every layer. Two things follow. Dense prediction needs features at several resolutions — detection heads and segmentation decoders were all built on the stride-4 to stride-32 pyramid a ResNet produces — and ViT has no pyramid to give them.

More binding still, global attention costs $O(n^2)$ in the number of tokens, and the number of tokens is quadratic in image side length. A $224\times224$ image is $196$ tokens; the $800\times1333$ inputs COCO detectors actually use, at a stride fine enough to localise small objects, run to tens of thousands. The attention matrix alone becomes the whole memory budget.

blocks.h: Windows, and the shift that connects them
blocks.b:
Swin partitions the feature map into non-overlapping $M \times M$ windows ($M=7$) and computes self-attention only within each. For an $h \times w$ map of width $C$ the cost falls from

$\Omega(\mathrm{MSA}) = 4hwC^{2} + 2(hw)^{2}C \quad\text{to}\quad \Omega(\mathrm{W\text{-}MSA}) = 4hwC^{2} + 2M^{2}hwC$

which is linear in $hw$ once $M$ is fixed. Windowing alone, though, leaves the partitions permanently isolated. The **shifted window** fixes this: every second block displaces the grid by $\lfloor M/2 \rfloor$ in both axes, so windows straddle the previous boundaries and a token's effective receptive field grows with depth. Naively this creates more, smaller windows at the edges; Swin instead applies a cyclic shift and masks the attention so that patches brought together only by wrap-around cannot attend to each other, keeping the batched window count constant. A learned relative position bias is added to the scores inside the softmax.

Between stages, a patch-merging layer concatenates each $2\times2$ group of neighbouring patches and projects the result, halving spatial resolution and doubling channel width — exactly the stride-and-widen schedule of a ResNet stage transition. Four stages give strides of $4$, $8$, $16$ and $32$, so a Swin backbone drops into an FPN, a Mask R-CNN head or an UperNet decoder with no adaptation.

This is what converted the architecture from an ImageNet result into infrastructure. Swin backbones took COCO box and mask AP and ADE20K mIoU well past the convolutional state of the art of the time, and for roughly two years a large fraction of the detection and segmentation leaderboard was Swin plus a head.

Locality, translation equivariance within a window, and a hand-chosen scale hierarchy are precisely the convolutional priors ViT had removed on the argument that enough data makes them unnecessary. Swin reintroduces them as engineering, with $M=7$, a shift of $M/2$ and a four-stage schedule all set by hand rather than learned.

ConvNeXt then made the awkward observation explicit: a ConvNet given Swin's macro design and training recipe matched it, which suggests the gains were as much structural as attentional. Meanwhile the original motive eroded from the other side — IO-aware exact attention made long global sequences affordable, and Swin V2 had to add post-norm, scaled cosine attention and a continuous log-spaced position bias before the design would scale to billions of parameters and much larger images.

refs.t: Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows
Swin Transformer V2: Scaling Up Capacity and Resolution

beit.lead: BEiT carried BERT's masked-prediction objective into vision by first giving images a discrete vocabulary. Patches are converted to indices by a separately trained visual tokeniser, a portion of them are hidden, and the Transformer is asked to name the missing tokens. It was the first demonstration that masked modelling — not contrastive learning — could pre-train a Vision Transformer well.

blocks.b:
BERT's recipe looks trivially portable: hide part of the input, predict it, keep the encoder. It had nonetheless failed repeatedly in vision, for a reason specific to the medium. Language arrives pre-discretised into a vocabulary of tens of thousands of types, so masked prediction is a classification problem with a well-posed answer. An image patch is a real-valued tensor whose exact contents are largely unpredictable noise — sensor grain, precise texture phase, lighting micro-variation. Regress raw pixels under a squared loss and the model spends most of its capacity on detail no downstream task cares about, converging to blurred means.

The practical alternative in 2021 was contrastive or distillation-based self-supervision — MoCo, SimCLR, BYOL, DINO — which sidesteps the issue by comparing whole views, but depends on a carefully tuned augmentation pipeline and large batches or momentum encoders.

BEiT's move is to make the target discrete before training. Every image gets two views of itself: a $14\times14$ grid of $16\times16$-pixel patches, which the ViT consumes, and a matching $14\times14$ grid of **visual tokens** produced by the discrete VAE released with DALL-E, whose codebook holds $8192$ entries. Around $40\%$ of the patch positions are masked — in contiguous blocks rather than independently, so the answer cannot be interpolated from immediate neighbours — and the masked positions are replaced with a learned embedding. The encoder output at each masked position goes through a linear head and a softmax over the codebook, trained with ordinary cross-entropy against the tokeniser's index.

The tokeniser is doing the work that matters. Its reconstruction bottleneck has already discarded the high-frequency content, so the objective is stated over a summarised, semantic-ish description of the patch rather than over pixels.

Fine-tuned, BEiT-pretrained ViTs beat both supervised-from-scratch training and the DINO-style self-supervised baselines of the day on ImageNet-1K classification and on ADE20K segmentation, with the margin widening at larger model size. Just as usefully, it stabilised the training of large ViTs, which had been notoriously fragile; the pre-trained initialisation removed much of the sensitivity to warmup and layer-scale tricks.

The attention maps that emerge are worth noting because nobody put them there: after pre-training with no labels at all, heads in the last layers separate objects from background, so a semantic grouping falls out of the reconstruction task alone. That result is what convinced the field that masked image modelling was a real pre-training paradigm rather than a curiosity.

The dependency BEiT relies on is also its weakest joint. The dVAE is an external model trained on a large private corpus with an unrelated objective, so the pre-training pipeline has two stages and the quality of stage two is capped by a codebook nobody optimised for representation learning. It is also lossy in the wrong direction: a purely reconstructive codebook preserves appearance, not semantics.

Everything after went at that seam. MAE showed the tokeniser could be dropped entirely if the mask ratio was raised far enough and the pixel targets normalised per patch. BEiT v2 kept the codebook but distilled it from CLIP features so the targets carried semantics. data2vec removed the discrete step altogether and regressed a momentum teacher's latent activations.

refs.t: BEiT: BERT Pre-Training of Image Transformers
Zero-Shot Text-to-Image Generation

mae.lead: MAE removed the tokeniser from masked image modelling and made the task hard instead: mask $75\%$ of the patches and reconstruct raw pixels. The encoder is shown only the visible quarter, and the mask tokens are handled by a small decoder that is thrown away afterwards — so an aggressive mask ratio makes pre-training cheaper rather than more expensive.

blocks.b:
BERT masks about $15\%$ of tokens because language is dense: removing a word usually removes information that must be recovered from syntax and meaning. Images are not dense. At $15\%$ masking a patch can be filled in by looking at what abuts it, and a model can score well on the objective with nothing but a learned interpolator — which is why early attempts at masked pixel prediction produced weak features.

MAE's answer is to raise the ratio until interpolation stops working. At $75\%$, and with the mask sampled uniformly at random so that holes are large, the visible context around a missing patch is too sparse for local extrapolation; the model must form some notion of what object it is looking at. The paper's ablation is unusually clean: representation quality rises with mask ratio up to about $75\%$ for both fine-tuning and linear probing, then falls.

The second idea is what makes the first affordable. Because a ViT is a set operation, masked positions can simply be deleted from the input sequence rather than substituted with a placeholder — an option a convolution does not have, since a conv kernel needs a value at every location. The encoder therefore runs over $25\%$ of the tokens and costs roughly a quarter as much per image.

Only at the decoder are mask tokens inserted, at their correct positional embeddings, into the full-length sequence. That decoder is deliberately narrow and shallow — a small fraction of the encoder's compute — and exists only to serve the reconstruction loss. Together these give more than a threefold wall-clock speedup over encoding every patch, which is how a ViT-Huge became practical to pre-train at all. Targets are per-patch normalised pixels; using the patch's own mean and variance measurably improves the learned features over raw intensities.

Pre-trained without labels on ImageNet-1K alone and then fine-tuned on that set's labels, with no external data at any stage, ViT-Huge reached $87.8\%$ top-1 — at the time the best result among methods using ImageNet-1K only, and a direct rebuttal of the claim that ViTs simply require JFT-scale labels. Crucially the benefit grew with model size, where supervised training on ImageNet-1K had long since saturated and begun to overfit. Transfer to COCO detection and ADE20K segmentation improved in step.

The practical consequence was that masked autoencoding became the default vision pre-training objective for the next several years, and the recipe ported almost unchanged to video, audio spectrograms and point clouds.

blocks.h: Linear probes and what they measure
blocks.b:
MAE's features are notably poor under linear probing relative to contrastive methods, and the paper does not hide it. The reason is structural: a contrastive objective explicitly pulls together augmented views of the same image and pushes apart different ones, which shapes the representation into linearly separable clusters, whereas reconstruction has no such pressure and can encode class information non-linearly. The authors argue the probe is therefore the wrong instrument, and introduce partial fine-tuning — unfreezing the last few blocks — to show the information is present and shallowly accessible.

The deeper gap is that MAE learns nothing about relations between images and nothing about language. iBOT and data2vec hybridised reconstruction with a teacher-matching term to recover probe performance; the larger shift was to CLIP-style image–text pre-training, which supplies exactly the cross-image, cross-modal structure a per-image reconstruction loss cannot.

refs.t: Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners

convnext.lead: ConvNeXt is an experiment written as an architecture. Starting from a ResNet-50 and changing one thing at a time towards Swin's design — while holding FLOPs roughly fixed and measuring after every step — it arrives at a pure convolutional network that matches or beats Swin on ImageNet, COCO and ADE20K. The finding is that most of what had been credited to self-attention was training recipe and macro design.

blocks.b:
By late 2021 Vision Transformers outperformed ResNets on essentially every benchmark, and the field had settled on an explanation: global, input-dependent attention is a better primitive than a static local kernel. The comparison supporting it was never clean. ViTs were trained for $300$ epochs with AdamW, heavy augmentation and regularisation, and modern schedules; the ResNet numbers being cited came from a $90$-epoch SGD recipe from 2015. Architecture and protocol had been varied together.

ConvNeXt separates them. The first step changes no architecture at all — AdamW, $300$ epochs, Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, random erasing, stochastic depth, label smoothing — and lifts ResNet-50 from $76.1\%$ to $78.8\%$ top-1. Close to three points, roughly half the gap to a Swin-T, existed before a single layer was touched.

What follows is a sequence of individually small changes, each kept only if it paid. Stage compute is rebalanced from $(3,4,6,3)$ blocks to $(3,3,9,3)$, matching Swin's $1{:}1{:}3{:}1$ ratio; the stem becomes a non-overlapping $4\times4$ stride-4 convolution, a patchify layer in all but name. The block goes depthwise, in ResNeXt's spirit, with the width increased to pay for the lost capacity, and is then inverted — a wide interior between narrow ends, as in MobileNetV2 and in a Transformer's MLP.

The depthwise convolution moves before the widening layer so the large kernel operates on few channels, and only then is the kernel enlarged. Benefit rises to $7\times7$ and stops, which is exactly Swin's window size. The micro-design changes are the ones people notice: ReLU to GELU, one activation and one normalisation per block instead of one per convolution, BatchNorm to LayerNorm, and separate downsampling convolutions with a normalisation in front to keep training stable.

ConvNeXt-T reaches about $82\%$ top-1 against Swin-T's $81.3\%$ at comparable FLOPs, and the ordering holds across the size range and up to $87.8\%$ for the largest model with ImageNet-22K pre-training. On COCO and ADE20K it is at least competitive with Swin backbones, and it is consistently a few percent faster at matched size — more at high resolution — because dense convolution kernels are better served by existing libraries than windowed attention with its cyclic shifts and masks.

The contribution is not the $0.7$ points. It is the demonstration that the ViT-versus-ConvNet comparison had been confounded, and a reminder that architectural claims need matched protocols — a methodological point the paper makes by construction rather than by argument.

blocks.h: What a kernel still cannot do
blocks.b:
Two differences survive the modernisation. A $7\times7$ depthwise kernel aggregates locally; global context is reached only by stacking, so the effective receptive field grows with depth rather than being available in one layer. And convolutional weights are static — the same filter applies whatever the input contains — whereas attention weights are computed from the data, which is what lets a Transformer route information conditionally and accept tokens from another modality on the same footing. That second property is why multimodal systems went to Transformers and stayed there, regardless of how the ImageNet numbers compared.

ConvNeXt V2 addressed a further gap: V1 did not take to masked pre-training, since masking breaks the translation structure convolutions assume. It required a fully convolutional MAE with sparse convolutions and a global response normalisation to prevent feature collapse. The large-kernel line continued separately, with RepLKNet pushing to $31\times31$.

refs.t: A ConvNet for the 2020s
ConvNeXt V2: Co-designing and Scaling ConvNets with Masked Autoencoders

inceptionv3.lead: Inception-v3 is the paper that tried to state, rather than merely exhibit, why the Inception module works. It replaces large convolutions with stacks and asymmetric pairs of smaller ones, fixes the grid-reduction step that had been either lossy or expensive, introduces label smoothing, and — quietly — retracts the original explanation of what the auxiliary classifiers were for.

blocks.b:
GoogLeNet was remarkably efficient for its accuracy: roughly $5$ million parameters and $1.5$ billion multiply-adds, against VGG's far heavier stack. But its topology was a thicket of hand-chosen branch counts and channel widths with no stated rationale, and it was known to be brittle — scale it naively, or alter one branch, and the efficiency evaporated. That made it nearly impossible to adapt to a new compute budget or a new domain, which is precisely what practitioners wanted to do.

Szegedy and colleagues therefore open with four design principles: avoid representational bottlenecks, particularly early in the network; higher-dimensional representations are easier to process locally; spatial aggregation can be done over a reduced-dimension embedding with little loss; and width and depth should be increased together. The rest of the paper is these principles applied.

A $5\times5$ convolution is replaced by two stacked $3\times3$ convolutions. The receptive field is identical and the parameter count per channel pair falls from $25$ to $18$, about $28\%$ cheaper, with an extra non-linearity gained rather than lost — using a linear first layer was tried and was worse.

The stronger form is asymmetric: an $n\times n$ convolution becomes a $1\times n$ followed by an $n\times1$, which for $n=3$ is a third cheaper than the square kernel. This turned out to be scale-dependent. On early, large feature maps it worked poorly; on medium grids around $12$ to $20$ across it worked well, and the network uses $1\times7$ and $7\times1$ pairs there. A third change concerns downsampling: pooling before expanding the width creates a bottleneck the principles forbid, while expanding first is expensive, so the reduction runs a stride-2 convolution branch and a stride-2 pooling branch in parallel and concatenates them.

Cross-entropy with a one-hot target is minimised only in the limit where the correct logit exceeds all others without bound, so the network is pushed towards over-confidence and towards gradients that keep pointing in the same direction. Label smoothing replaces the target with a mixture,

$q'(k) = (1-\epsilon)\,\delta_{k,y} + \epsilon/K$

with $\epsilon = 0.1$ over $K = 1000$ classes: a small fixed mass is spread uniformly over the wrong labels. The gain reported was a few tenths of a point on ImageNet, which understates its influence — it is now standard in classification and in machine translation, where the Transformer uses the same $\epsilon$.

The auxiliary classifiers are handled with equal candour. GoogLeNet had justified them as a way of injecting gradient into the lower layers; here the authors observe that removing the lower head changes nothing, and that the remaining head helps only near convergence. Their effect is regularisation, not gradient flow, which is why the branch benefits from batch normalisation or dropout.

The result was around $21\%$ top-1 and $5.6\%$ top-5 single-crop error on ILSVRC-2012 at roughly $5$ billion multiply-adds, with an ensemble reaching about $3.5\%$ top-5 — competitive with far costlier models, and Inception-v3 became for several years the default ImageNet feature extractor and the backbone behind the Inception Score and FID.

What it did not achieve is the generality its own principles promised. The network still consists of three distinct module types with hand-tuned channel counts, an idiosyncratic stem, and a grid-reduction block chosen by experiment. Nothing about it transfers by rule to a different budget. ResNet sidestepped the problem with a uniform repeated block; NASNet attacked it directly, searching for an Inception-like cell instead of designing one.

refs.t: Rethinking the Inception Architecture for Computer Vision

inceptionv4.lead: This paper asks a question that had gone unexamined: does the Inception family actually need residual connections? It builds a cleaned-up pure-Inception network and hybrid Inception-ResNet variants side by side, and finds that residuals accelerate training substantially while final accuracy at matched cost is much the same. Along the way it identifies and fixes a failure mode of wide residual networks.

blocks.h: Two legacies, tested against each other
blocks.b:
By 2016 the Inception line and the residual line had solved overlapping problems by unrelated means. Inception controlled cost by factorising convolutions and branching over multiple kernel sizes; ResNet made very deep networks optimisable by giving gradients an identity path. The two had never been separated experimentally, and the prevailing story — that residual connections are what allow depth and hence accuracy — had not been tested against a strong non-residual baseline.

A second, more prosaic constraint had also lifted. The earlier Inception designs were shaped in part by having to partition a model across replicas under DistBelief, which forced compromises in module layout. With TensorFlow's memory optimisation for backpropagation the constraint was gone, so the authors could first do what the previous architectures had never permitted: make the design uniform. Inception-v4 is that network — one stem, and repeated blocks of three kinds with a consistent reduction between them.

The hybrid replaces each block's filter concatenation with an addition. An Inception branch reduces dimensionality by design, so a $1\times1$ convolution — a filter-expansion layer, deliberately without an activation — restores the width to match the incoming tensor before the residual sum. Batch normalisation is applied on the conventional layers but not on the summations, purely so that the model fits in memory at the sizes being trained.

The striking practical result is the learning curve. Inception-ResNet-v1 and -v2 reach a given error in noticeably fewer epochs than their non-residual counterparts of comparable cost, but the curves converge: Inception-v4 finishes close to Inception-ResNet-v2. **The residual connection buys optimisation speed rather than representational capacity here**, at least at this depth — a useful qualification of the ResNet narrative, since these networks are not thousands of layers deep and were trainable without shortcuts.

The instability the paper reports is specific and worth knowing. When the residual branches carried more than roughly a thousand filters, training died: after tens of thousands of iterations the layer before the average pooling began producing only zeros, and the network never recovered. Lowering the learning rate did not prevent it, and adding batch normalisation to the affected layers did not either.

The fix is to scale the residual branch down by a constant, somewhere between $0.1$ and $0.3$, before adding it to the identity path. This narrows the branch's contribution at initialisation, keeping the block near the identity until the weights have organised. He and colleagues had used a two-phase warm-up for the same purpose; the authors found scaling more reliable and less sensitive to how the warm-up was configured. The same trick reappears later as LayerScale and as the residual initialisation schemes used in large Transformers.

blocks.h: The end of the hand-designed stack
blocks.b:
An ensemble of one Inception-v4 and three Inception-ResNet-v2 models reached $3.1\%$ top-5 error on the ILSVRC-2012 validation set and $3.08\%$ on the test set, then the best published result, and Inception-ResNet-v2 remained a standard high-accuracy backbone for some years.

It was also close to the end of this style of work. The architecture is a long list of block diagrams whose channel counts have no derivation, and the scaling constant is one more free hyperparameter with no theory behind it. Within two years the field had moved to designs that are either uniform and scalable — ResNeXt, DenseNet — or searched rather than drawn, as in NASNet, which took Inception's branching cell as its search space. The idea from Inception that actually persisted was Xception's rereading of it: that the module approximates a depthwise separable convolution, the primitive on which MobileNet and EfficientNet were built.

refs.t: Inception-v4, Inception-ResNet and the Impact of Residual Connections on Learning

sknet.lead: SKNet makes a convolutional unit choose its own receptive-field size, per channel and per input. Two branches with different kernel sizes are fused, summarised by global pooling, and recombined with softmax weights computed from that summary — so a layer can favour a wide kernel for a large object and a narrow one for a small one, instead of committing to one scale at design time.

blocks.h: A fixed receptive field is a design-time guess
blocks.b:
Every convolutional layer commits to a kernel size before it sees any data, and that choice sets the scale at which the layer can integrate evidence. Objects, however, arrive at wildly different scales within a single dataset and often within a single image. Inception acknowledged this by running several kernel sizes in parallel — but it concatenates their outputs and lets the next layer's fixed weights combine them, so the mixture is learned once and applied identically to every input thereafter.

SENet had by then shown that a cheap global descriptor can be used to reweight channels dynamically. SKNet's observation is that the same mechanism can be pointed at a different axis: instead of asking which channels matter for this image, ask which receptive field size matters. The motivation cited is the finding in visual neuroscience that a cortical neuron's receptive field size is not fixed but modulated by the stimulus.

The unit runs the input through two transforms with different kernel sizes — $3\times3$ and $5\times5$, the latter implemented as a $3\times3$ dilated by $2$ for efficiency, both grouped and each followed by batch normalisation and ReLU. Their outputs $\tilde{U}$ and $\hat{U}$ are summed and globally average-pooled to a channel descriptor $s$, which a bottleneck fully-connected layer compresses to $d = \max(C/r, L)$ dimensions with $r = 16$ and $L = 32$.

Two linear maps $A$ and $B$ then produce per-branch, per-channel logits, and a softmax across branches gives the gate. For channel $c$,

$a_c = \dfrac{e^{A_c z}}{e^{A_c z} + e^{B_c z}}, \qquad V_c = a_c \tilde{U}_c + (1-a_c)\hat{U}_c$

so the branch weights sum to one and the unit interpolates continuously between kernel sizes. Strip out the second branch and what remains is SE's own skeleton — global descriptor, bottleneck FC, per-channel gate — with a sigmoid over one path in place of a softmax across two, which places SK precisely in that lineage.

blocks.h: Evidence the gate does what it claims
blocks.b:
Substituted for the large-kernel convolutions of a ResNeXt-50 backbone, SK units improved ImageNet top-1 by more than a point at comparable parameter count and computation, and the gain held for deeper variants and for lightweight backbones such as ShuffleNet — a stronger signal than the raw number, since attention modules frequently fail to transfer between capacity regimes.

The more interesting experiment enlarges the central object of a validation image by resizing it and watches the gate. The weight assigned to the $5\times5$ branch rises monotonically with object size, which is the behaviour the design predicts and is not something the loss was told to produce. The effect is clear in the middle and later stages and weakest at the very last stage, where the spatial resolution is already too small for the two kernels to differ much.

blocks.h: What it moved rather than removed
blocks.b:
The hand-designed choice is relocated rather than eliminated: the network selects among receptive fields, but the menu of receptive fields — how many branches, which kernel sizes, which dilation — is still fixed by the designer. Running multiple branches also costs real compute, most of which is discarded by the gate, and the branch weight is derived from a globally pooled descriptor, so the selection is uniform across the feature map. An image containing a large object and a small one cannot have different kernels applied in different places, which is the case the mechanism was motivated by.

ResNeSt generalised the construction to attention across feature-map groups; CondConv and dynamic convolution went further and made the kernel weights themselves a data-dependent mixture. The broader idea — that aggregation weights should be computed from the input rather than fixed — is what self-attention supplies in full generality, and the ViT line absorbed it.

refs.t: Selective Kernel Networks
Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks

maxvit.lead: MaxViT decomposes global self-attention into two sparse forms, each linear in the number of pixels: block attention inside local windows, and grid attention over a sparsely sampled global lattice. Stacked as a pair after an MBConv, they give every layer both a local and a global receptive field, at any input resolution.

blocks.b:
Swin made attention affordable by confining it to $7\times7$ windows and recovering cross-window flow by shifting the partition on alternate blocks. Information then propagates by diffusion: pixels at opposite corners of the image are many blocks apart, and the depth needed to connect them grows with input resolution — awkward precisely where a hierarchical backbone is supposed to earn its keep, in detection and segmentation at high resolution.

The shift also brings machinery: cyclic rolls, attention masks at the seams, padding when the map is not divisible by the window. MaxViT's wager is that what is missing is not more shifting but a **second, complementary sparsity** — a partition whose windows are global by construction, rather than local ones nudged around.

A feature map $X \in \mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C}$ is attended twice, under two reshapes. Block attention views it as $(\tfrac{H}{P}\times\tfrac{W}{P},\, P\times P,\, C)$ and attends within each $P\times P$ tile: dense and local. Grid attention views it as $(G\times G,\, \tfrac{H}{G}\times\tfrac{W}{G},\, C)$ and attends across the leading axis — pixels sampled on a dilated lattice of stride $H/G$, spread uniformly over the whole image: sparse and global.

With $P$ and $G$ both fixed at $7$, each attention runs over $49$ elements and both cost $O(HW)$ rather than $O((HW)^2)$. The pair is a decomposition of full attention along two axes, local and global, much as axial attention decomposes it along rows and columns.

Each MaxViT block runs an MBConv with squeeze-and-excitation before the two attentions, and not merely for the sake of being a hybrid. The depthwise convolution supplies the local inductive bias that lets the model train competitively on ImageNet-1k alone instead of needing a JFT-scale corpus, and it acts as a conditional position encoding, which is why the network carries no absolute positional embedding — attention adds only a relative bias.

Downsampling happens in the MBConv, giving the usual four-stage pyramid. The payoff is a single repeated unit — convolution, local attention, global attention — that stacks uniformly, in place of the stage-specific designs earlier hierarchical transformers required.

blocks.h: What it bought, and what it costs
blocks.b:
Trained on ImageNet-1k with no extra data MaxViT passes 85% top-1, and with large-scale pre-training it approaches 90%; it transfers well to detection and segmentation, and the paper also stands the backbone up as a GAN generator, which is a fair test of whether the global mixing is real.

Two costs remain. The block layout — stage depths, where the MBConv sits, the fixed $P = G = 7$ — is hand-set, and the grid stride is tied to input resolution, so changing resolution changes what the global branch samples. And the two reshapes are memory-bound permutes, so measured latency lags the linear FLOP count. Later work often preferred plain global attention at low resolution with an IO-aware kernel, which removes the layout question entirely.

refs.t: MaxViT: Multi-Axis Vision Transformer
Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows

coatnet.lead: CoAtNet unifies depthwise convolution and self-attention by adding a translation-invariant relative bias to the attention logits before the softmax, so one operator contains both. It then stacks them in a fixed vertical order — convolution in the high-resolution stages, attention in the low-resolution ones — on the argument that generalisation and capacity are wanted at different depths.

blocks.b:
ViT beat comparable ResNets only after pre-training on JFT-300M; on ImageNet-1k alone it trailed them, because nothing in the architecture encodes locality or translation equivariance and both must be learned from examples. A convolution has them built in and therefore generalises from far less data, but the same static kernel bounds what the layer can express: the weights do not depend on the input, so a ConvNet's returns flatten as the corpus grows.

The paper states this as a two-term trade — **generalisation versus capacity** — and takes the position that neither operator should be chosen outright. The question is where in the network each one is worth its price.

The unifying operator is a global relative attention in which a learned scalar depending only on the offset is added to the content score before normalisation:

$y_i = \sum_{j\in\mathcal{G}} \frac{\exp\!\left(x_i^{\top}x_j + w_{i-j}\right)}{\sum_{k\in\mathcal{G}}\exp\!\left(x_i^{\top}x_k + w_{i-k}\right)}\, x_j$

Here $\mathcal{G}$ is the whole feature map, $x_i^{\top}x_j$ is the usual content-dependent term, and $w_{i-j}$ is indexed by the relative position alone — that is, a convolution kernel. Delete the dot product and the layer is a depthwise convolution with softmax-normalised weights; delete $w$ and it is ordinary attention.

Because the bias enters before normalisation rather than being mixed in afterwards, the static kernel and the adaptive term compete inside one distribution, and $w$ costs only one parameter per offset.

With five stages $S_0$–$S_4$, the paper enumerates four vertical layouts — C-C-C-C, C-C-C-T, C-C-T-T, C-T-T-T — and tests them on two axes. Generalisation, measured by how a given training loss transfers to held-out accuracy, degrades monotonically as transformer blocks replace convolutional ones. Capacity, measured by fit on JFT, moves the other way. C-C-T-T and C-T-T-T tie on capacity, and a transfer test between them decides for C-C-T-T.

There is a hard practical reason underneath the search. Global attention at stride 4 or 8 is quadratically unaffordable, so the MBConv stages must carry the image down to $1/16$ before attention can be global at all.

blocks.h: Results and the hyperparameter left behind
blocks.b:
Without extra data CoAtNet reaches 86.0% top-1, and with ImageNet-21k pre-training 88.56% — matching JFT-300M-pretrained ViT-Huge at roughly 23x less pre-training compute; with JFT-3B it set the ImageNet record of its moment at 90.88%. It made the hybrid respectable again after a year in which the field had read ViT as evidence that convolution was dispensable.

What it does not do is decide the seam automatically. C-C-T-T is a discrete choice fixed once and implicitly conditioned on input resolution and dataset size; nothing in the model adapts it. The transformer stages also still perform full attention, which keeps high-resolution dense prediction expensive — the thread a different Google team picked up a year later in MaxViT.

refs.t: CoAtNet: Marrying Convolution and Attention for All Data Sizes
An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale

efficientformer.lead: EfficientFormer asks what a vision transformer costs in milliseconds on a phone rather than in multiply-adds, and rebuilds the architecture around the answer. Its smallest model reaches 79.2% top-1 on ImageNet-1k at about 1.6 ms on an iPhone 12 — MobileNet latency from a transformer, which the prevailing wisdom held was not available.

blocks.b:
The efficient-ViT literature optimised parameter count and FLOPs, and the resulting models were still slower on device than MobileNetV2. Profiling on an iPhone 12 through CoreML located the causes, and none of them is the attention matrix.

Patch embedding with a large-kernel, large-stride convolution is poorly supported by mobile compilers. Frequent reshapes between 4D feature maps and 3D token sequences — which every hybrid performs at each stage boundary — cost more than the operators between them. LayerNorm and GELU are evaluated per token and cannot be folded away, whereas BatchNorm collapses into the preceding convolution at export time. **The tensor layout, not the token mixer, is what the hardware charges for.**

The network is therefore split into a 4D partition and a 3D partition with exactly one reshape between them, at one point in the whole forward pass. Early stages use a 4D block: a pooling token mixer with convolution and BatchNorm, everything staying in NCHW. The final stage, at $1/32$ resolution, uses a 3D block with genuine multi-head self-attention, LayerNorm and linear projections over a flattened sequence — short enough that the quadratic term is negligible. The stem is two stride-2 $3\times3$ convolutions rather than a single patchify convolution.

Each of these follows from the profiler rather than from an accuracy ablation, which is the point: the architecture is derived from the deployment target.

Width and depth are then chosen by search. A supernet allows each block position to be a 4D pooling block, a 3D attention block, or skipped, and candidates are scored against a lookup table of latencies measured on the target phone rather than against a proxy cost. The search shrinks per-stage width and depth until the latency budget binds.

That produced the L1, L3 and L7 family spanning roughly MobileNet to server-class accuracy, with L7 above 83% top-1 at single-digit milliseconds. The contribution is less any one block than the demonstration that a latency objective and a FLOP objective select genuinely different architectures.

The result is conditioned on one device and one compiler. A latency table for an iPhone 12 under CoreML does not transfer to a server GPU, another NPU, or a later toolchain, so the architecture is optimal against a target that moves without warning — an uncomfortable property for a published backbone.

Confining attention to the last stage also means global mixing happens only at $1/32$ resolution, which is thin for dense prediction; detection and segmentation results were respectable rather than where the model's advantage lies. EfficientFormerV2 went after both, reworking the search to trade size and latency jointly and pushing attention into earlier stages with downsampled keys and values.

refs.t: EfficientFormer: Vision Transformers at MobileNet Speed

convnext2.lead: ConvNeXt V2 asks what a ConvNet must change to be pre-trained the way MAE pre-trains a ViT, and finds two things. Masking has to be implemented as sparse convolution so the encoder never touches a masked pixel, and the block needs a new normaliser, GRN, to stop channels collapsing onto each other under a reconstruction objective.

blocks.b:
MAE removes masked patches from the encoder input altogether. A ViT is a set function, so this is free, and keeping a quarter of the tokens costs roughly a quarter of the compute. A ConvNet cannot do it. A dense convolution slides over whatever occupies the masked positions, so the mask pattern leaks into every subsequent activation and the network learns to detect it. Substituting a learned mask token — the alternative — discards the compute saving and introduces a train-test distribution shift at every layer.

The paper's starting observation is not a hypothetical: dropping ConvNeXt into the MAE recipe unmodified performed worse than plain supervised training.

FCMAE treats the visible pixels as a sparse tensor and runs the encoder's convolutions as submanifold sparse convolutions, which produce output only where input exists. Masking then becomes exact — no receptive field ever crosses into a masked region — and the compute saving returns. At fine-tuning the identical weights run as ordinary dense convolutions, with no conversion step.

The decoder is deliberately trivial, a single ConvNeXt block predicting pixels, since capacity spent there is capacity not spent in the encoder one actually keeps. Masking is aggressive and blockwise, around 60% in large square regions, because on a locally correlated pixel grid a scattered low-ratio mask is reconstructible by interpolation from neighbours and teaches nothing.

Inspecting an FCMAE-trained encoder turned up many near-dead channels and high cosine similarity between the surviving ones, concentrated in the expanded MLP of each block. Global Response Normalization rescales each channel by its response relative to all channels:

$$\hat{X}_i = \gamma\, X_i \cdot \frac{\lVert X_i \rVert_2}{\frac{1}{C}\sum_{j=1}^{C}\lVert X_j \rVert_2} + \beta + X_i$$

where $\lVert X_i \rVert_2$ is the spatial L2 norm of channel $i$ and $\gamma,\beta$ are learned. A channel responding below the average is damped, one above is amplified: explicit competition between channels, in the spirit of lateral inhibition and the long-abandoned local response normalisation. It replaces LayerScale in the block.

The two pieces only work together. GRN adds little to supervised training, and FCMAE without GRN loses to supervision; together they turn the deficit into a gain across a family spanning roughly 3.7M to 650M parameters, with the largest model reaching 88.9% top-1 on ImageNet using only publicly available data. That range is the practical result — masked pre-training that pays off at the tiny end, where MAE-style ViTs had little to offer.

The costs are a dependency on sparse-convolution kernels and a long pre-training schedule. And the larger question is untouched: image-text pre-training standardised on ViTs, so parity on pixel reconstruction did not win the ConvNet back a place in the multimodal stack.

refs.t: ConvNeXt V2: Co-designing and Scaling ConvNets with Masked Autoencoders
Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners

inceptionnext.lead: InceptionNeXt starts from a measurement rather than an idea: ConvNeXt's $7\times7$ depthwise convolution is almost free in FLOPs and expensive in wall-clock, because depthwise convolution is memory-bound. Splitting it across channels into a small square kernel, two orthogonal band kernels and an identity branch keeps the large effective receptive field and restores throughput.

blocks.h: A cheap layer that runs slowly
blocks.b:
ConvNeXt took the large kernel from Swin's window size, and on paper a $7\times7$ depthwise convolution is a rounding error — a few percent of the block's multiply-adds. In practice it is one of the slowest things in the network. Depthwise convolution has no channel reuse: with no reduction over input channels, each activation it loads feeds only $k^2$ multiply-accumulates instead of the $k^2C_{\text{out}}$ a dense convolution extracts, so arithmetic intensity per byte moved is close to the floor and the layer is bound by memory bandwidth while the arithmetic units idle.

Going from $3\times3$ to $7\times7$ therefore buys accuracy at a throughput cost far out of proportion to its FLOPs, and simply shrinking the kernel back gives the accuracy away. The trade looked forced.

blocks.h: Four branches over a channel split
blocks.b:
The block partitions its channels instead. A small group passes through a $3\times3$ depthwise convolution; two further groups pass through $1\times k$ and $k\times1$ band kernels with $k=11$; the remaining majority is an identity branch, concatenated straight back.

The bands supply the spatial extent — a $1\times11$ kernel spans as far as a large square kernel along one axis at cost linear in $k$ rather than quadratic. The identity branch is the load-bearing part: most channels get no spatial mixing in this layer at all, and the pointwise MLP that follows redistributes information across channels regardless. This is **Inception-v3's factorisation of $n\times n$ into $1\times n$ and $n\times1$**, applied in parallel across the channel axis rather than in sequence along depth.

The justification is redundancy. A depthwise layer's channels are independent spatial filters, and in a trained network a large fraction of them settle into broad, low-frequency responses that a small kernel or a band approximates well; only some need the full square support. Convolving a modest fraction of channels is enough, provided the ones that are convolved cover both a compact neighbourhood and a long axis.

Measured, InceptionNeXt-T slightly exceeds ConvNeXt-T's ImageNet-1k accuracy at roughly $1.6\times$ its training throughput. The token mixer is a drop-in substitution, so the same replacement carries into other MetaFormer-shaped backbones without touching the rest of the design.

The channel split ratio and the band length are hand-set constants, chosen by inspection rather than searched, and nothing ties them to depth or stage resolution — the natural next question the paper does not answer.

The speed claim is also a claim about particular hardware. It rests on depthwise convolution being bandwidth-bound and on slicing and concatenation being cheap; on accelerators where depthwise kernels are well served, or where the channel shuffle is not free, the accounting changes. And the result is throughput rather than accuracy, arriving at a point when the field's returns had moved decisively from backbone design to pre-training scale — which is why a genuinely useful efficiency result attracted less attention than it might have in 2019.

refs.t: InceptionNeXt: When Inception Meets ConvNeXt
A ConvNet for the 2020s

mask2former.lead: Mask2Former took MaskFormer's mask-classification formulation and made it beat the specialised architectures it was meant to replace, on panoptic, instance and semantic segmentation at once. The change that names it is a one-line edit to the decoder's cross-attention: a query attends only inside the mask it predicted at the previous layer, never over the whole image.

blocks.h: Universal in form, not in results
blocks.b:
Semantic segmentation was per-pixel classification; instance and panoptic segmentation needed proposals or grouping heuristics, so three tasks were served by three families of model. MaskFormer had shown the unification a few months earlier: predict a fixed set of $N$ binary masks, each with one class label, and read semantic or panoptic output off the same predictions by different post-processing.

The formulation was clean and the numbers were not. MaskFormer was competitive on semantic segmentation but trailed the Mask R-CNN line on instance segmentation, and it was expensive to train — long schedules, and a loss evaluated over full-resolution masks for every query. **An architecture that loses to the specialists on two tasks out of three does not replace them**, whatever its conceptual tidiness.

blocks.h: Attention confined to its own mask
blocks.b:
A standard Transformer decoder lets every query cross-attend to every location of the image feature map. Early in training that context is almost entirely background, and the query has no reason to converge on any particular object. Mask2Former restricts the attention to the query's own current prediction:

$$X_l = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\mathcal{M}_{l-1} + Q_l K_l^{\top}\right)V_l + X_{l-1}$$

where $\mathcal{M}_{l-1}$ is an additive mask that is $0$ at locations the previous layer's mask predicted as foreground and $-\infty$ everywhere else. The previous prediction is thresholded and resized to the resolution of the features the layer attends over; the first layer uses a mask produced from the learnable query features themselves. The effect is local features from the start, and convergence in a fraction of the schedule MaskFormer needed.

blocks.h: The rest of the decoder, retuned
blocks.b: Masked attention alone was not enough. Small objects need resolution, so the pixel decoder emits features at $1/32$, $1/16$ and $1/8$ and successive decoder layers consume them in rotation, each query passing through all three scales repeatedly. The order of the sub-layers is inverted — cross-attention first, then self-attention — because the query features entering layer one are image-independent, so self-attention over them can carry no information about the image. The query features are learnable and directly supervised, acting as a region proposal rather than a positional slot. Dropout was removed from the decoder. Finally, the mask loss is computed on a sampled subset of points, following the PointRend line, instead of on every pixel of every mask, which cut training memory several-fold and made the training cost tractable.

One architecture with one set of hyper-parameters set the state of the art on COCO panoptic, COCO instance and ADE20K semantic segmentation simultaneously, and held up on Cityscapes and Mapillary Vistas. That combination is what ended the argument: after Mask2Former, a query-based mask-classification head became the default assumption for new segmentation work, and box-and-mask pipelines stopped being the obvious baseline. The design transferred almost unchanged to video instance segmentation by letting queries attend across frames, and it became the segmentation component of later systems — Mask DINO folding in detection-style denoising and query selection, OneFormer conditioning the same decoder on a task token.

The architecture is universal; the model is not. Mask2Former is still trained separately for each task and each dataset, and OneFormer's contribution was precisely to train one set of weights jointly. Masked attention is also self-referential: evidence outside the current mask reaches the query only indirectly, through the residual stream and the pixel decoder, so a query that latches onto the wrong region recovers slowly, and thin structures and small objects remain the weak point. And the label set is closed — a fixed classifier over a fixed taxonomy. Open-vocabulary and promptable segmentation, from X-Decoder to SAM, went after that limitation rather than this one.

refs.t: Masked-attention Mask Transformer for Universal Image Segmentation
Per-Pixel Classification is Not All You Need for Semantic Segmentation

attnunet.lead: Attention U-Net puts a small gating module on each of U-Net's skip connections, so that encoder features are multiplied by a learned spatial map of relevance before they are concatenated into the decoder. It was written for one concrete failure — segmenting the pancreas in abdominal CT, a small organ of highly variable shape that a plain U-Net surrounds with false positives — and it removed the localise-then-segment cascade that was the standard remedy.

blocks.h: The cascade it was written to remove
blocks.b:
A U-Net skip connection carries high-resolution features from an early encoder stage straight across to the decoder. Those features have had very little processing, so they represent background tissue as faithfully as foreground. When the target occupies a small and shifting fraction of the volume, as an abdominal organ does, the decoder inherits far more irrelevant evidence than relevant, and the failure shows up as scattered false positives in neighbouring tissue.

The accepted fix was a multi-stage pipeline: one network localises the organ or produces a coarse region of interest, a second segments inside the crop. It works, at the cost of duplicated parameters, a separate training procedure, and a hard decision made once — anything the localiser misses is unrecoverable downstream.

blocks.h: An additive gate on every skip
blocks.b:
The attention gate scores each spatial location of the skip tensor $x$ against a gating signal $g$ taken from the coarser decoder level below it:

$$\alpha = \sigma\!\left(\psi^{\top}\,\mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(W_x^{\top}x + W_g^{\top}g + b\right)\right)$$

and the skip features are passed on as $\alpha \odot x$. Two choices matter. The nonlinearity that produces $\alpha$ is a sigmoid, not a softmax, so several disjoint regions may be kept at once and the map is not forced to sum to one. And $\alpha$ is a grid — one coefficient per spatial location — rather than a single vector per image, which is what lets it suppress a region instead of reweighting a channel. Because the gate multiplies the forward activations, it also scales the gradients flowing back into the encoder, so it shapes what the encoder learns and not only what the decoder sees.

blocks.h: Why the gating signal comes from below
blocks.b: The gate could have been driven by the skip features themselves. It is driven instead by the coarser decoder activation, which has passed through more of the network and therefore already carries a rough sense of where the object is. That makes the arrangement coarse-to-fine: the decision at $1/16$ resolution constrains what survives at $1/8$, and so on, which is the cascade's logic folded into one differentiable pass. Additive attention was chosen over the cheaper multiplicative form on accuracy grounds. Deep supervision is applied at intermediate resolutions so the gates receive a training signal that is not diluted by depth, and the paper notes that without it the intermediate maps are less interpretable and less useful.

blocks.h: Modest gains, and the awkward later verdict
blocks.b: On CT pancreas data the gates gave a few points of Dice over the same U-Net without them, for a small parameter increase and a single forward pass instead of a cascade. The module is architecture-agnostic, and it was duly bolted onto many later U-Net variants. What it does not provide is context: $\alpha$ is a per-location scalar, so distant regions never interact the way self-attention would, and the gate can only suppress what the encoder already computed. The harder verdict came from nnU-Net, which found that a plain U-Net with a properly configured preprocessing and training pipeline matched or beat most published architectural variants — placing the burden of proof on modules like this one. Receptive field was then attacked directly, by TransUNet, UNETR and Swin-UNet.

refs.t: Attention U-Net: Learning Where to Look for the Pancreas

swin2.lead: Swin-v2 is not a new architecture so much as a set of repairs that let the Swin design be trained at 3 billion parameters and at input resolutions up to $1536 \times 1536$. Three of them are structural — post-norm on the residual branch, cosine attention with a learned temperature, and a log-spaced continuous position bias — and each targets a failure that only appears once you try to scale.

blocks.h: Three failures that only appear at scale
blocks.b:
The first is instability. In a pre-norm Transformer each block adds its output directly into the residual stream, so activation amplitudes accumulate with depth; at large model size the discrepancy between the deepest and shallowest layers grows by orders of magnitude, and in mixed precision the deep layers overflow and training collapses.

The second is degenerate attention. With dot-product scores, some heads at large size were found to be dominated by a handful of pixel pairs, the softmax concentrating on them and the rest of the window contributing nothing.

The third is transfer. Swin's relative position bias is a lookup table indexed by relative offset within a window; moving from low-resolution pretraining to high-resolution fine-tuning changes the window size, and the table has to be interpolated into a range it never saw, which cost accuracy.

For the first, Swin-v2 moves the LayerNorm from the input of each residual branch to its output, so what is added into the main branch is always normalised and amplitudes stop compounding with depth. In the largest models an extra LayerNorm is inserted every few blocks as well.

For the second, the dot product is replaced by a cosine similarity with a learnable, non-shared temperature:

$$\mathrm{Sim}(q_i, k_j) = \frac{\cos(q_i, k_j)}{\tau} + B_{ij}$$

Since cosine similarity is bounded in $[-1,1]$ regardless of how large the query and key norms become, no pair can dominate the softmax through sheer magnitude, and $\tau$ — learned per head, floored to keep it from collapsing — sets how sharp the distribution is allowed to be. Both changes are cheap and neither alters the shape of the computation.

blocks.h: Position bias as a function, not a table
blocks.b:
The third fix replaces the bias table with a small network. A two-layer MLP maps a relative coordinate to its bias, so the bias is defined continuously and any window size can be evaluated, including sizes never trained on. On top of that the coordinates are compressed logarithmically before being fed in,

$$\widehat{\Delta x} = \mathrm{sign}(\Delta x)\cdot\log\!\left(1 + |\Delta x|\right)$$

which matters because the extrapolation that hurts is in the input range of that network. Going from an $8\times8$ window to a $16\times16$ one nearly doubles the linear offset range, but in log coordinates the required extrapolation is a small fraction of that. Pretrain at low resolution, fine-tune at high, and the bias transfers with far less loss.

blocks.h: What it took to actually run
blocks.b: The remaining obstacles were engineering and data. Memory at $1536^2$ was handled with the zero-redundancy optimiser, activation checkpointing, and a sequential self-attention implementation used only for the largest configurations. Labelled data was the other constraint: rather than assemble a proprietary billion-image labelled corpus, the authors leaned on SimMIM, a masked-image-modelling objective, so a 3B-parameter model could be pretrained from a comparatively modest labelled set. The resulting SwinV2-G set records across ImageNet-V2 classification, COCO detection, ADE20K segmentation and Kinetics video, which was the point: the fixes were justified by the scale they made reachable, not by an accuracy gain at the old size.

Every fix here was found by diagnosing a symptom, and none comes with a theory that predicts where the next instability will appear. The architecture also keeps window attention, so a single layer still has no global receptive field and the shifted-window scheme remains the only mixing path between windows. More pointedly, the case for hierarchy itself weakened shortly afterwards: ViTDet showed a plain, non-hierarchical ViT with a trivially constructed feature pyramid to be competitive on detection, and masked pretraining proved to work well on plain ViTs, which removed one of the main arguments for the extra machinery Swin carries.

refs.t: Swin Transformer V2: Scaling Up Capacity and Resolution
SimMIM: A Simple Framework for Masked Image Modeling

cvt.lead: CvT puts convolutions back into two places inside a vision Transformer: the tokenisation, which becomes a strided overlapping convolution applied at the start of each of three stages, and the query/key/value projection, which becomes a depthwise separable convolution instead of a linear map. The consequence the paper leans on hardest is a deletion — with convolution supplying locality and order, the position embedding can be removed entirely with no loss.

blocks.h: What ViT gave up to be pure
blocks.b: ViT's design argument was that a Transformer with no vision-specific prior would win once given enough data, and on JFT-300M it did. On ImageNet-1k alone it did not, and DeiT's answer was a training recipe — heavy augmentation and distillation — rather than an architectural one. Three costs of the purity remained. The patch embedding is a non-overlapping stride-16 projection, so nothing models the continuity across a patch boundary. The token grid never changes resolution, so the model has one scale throughout and no cheap way to spend capacity where detail is. And the learned position embedding is a table with one row per patch position, tied to the training resolution and requiring interpolation for anything else.

CvT replaces the single tokenisation with three. At the start of each stage the token sequence is reshaped back into a 2D map and passed through a convolution with kernel larger than its stride, which overlaps neighbouring patches, reduces the spatial size, and increases the channel width. The result is the CNN's familiar trade — fewer tokens, richer each — expressed as a re-tokenisation, and it gives the Transformer a pyramid without a separate downsampling mechanism. Because the convolution is applied over a spatial grid with a fixed kernel, adjacency is baked into every token: two tokens that were neighbours share input pixels. That is the property the model then exploits to drop position embeddings, and the ablation is explicit — removing them costs nothing here, while removing them from a plain ViT is severely damaging.

blocks.h: Convolutional projection, and the free saving
blocks.b: Inside each attention block, the linear map that produces queries, keys and values is replaced by a depthwise separable convolution over the reshaped token map. This adds local context to each token's projection at negligible parameter cost, and it opens a cheap efficiency lever: the convolutions producing keys and values are given stride $2$, so attention is computed against roughly a quarter as many key–value tokens as query tokens. **The cost of attention drops by about four times while every query still produces its own output**, which is the same asymmetric-resolution idea PVT reached by a different route. The reported accuracy loss from the subsampling is small, and the saving is what makes the higher-resolution early stages affordable.

blocks.h: Results and the argument it fed
blocks.b: CvT reached above 81% ImageNet-1k top-1 with roughly 20M parameters, trained without external data and without distillation, which put it ahead of comparable DeiT models at similar size; larger variants pretrained on ImageNet-22k extended the pattern. Removing the position embedding also made variable input resolution natural, which matters for transfer to dense prediction. The wider effect was to shift the debate: after CvT, PVTv2, and the several contemporaneous hybrids, a convolutional stem and overlapping patches became standard, and the pure-attention claim survived mainly at very large data scales.

blocks.h: The prior is a crutch at some scale
blocks.b: A locality prior helps most when data is scarce and matters least when it is not, so the ImageNet-1k comparison flatters the hybrid in a way that does not necessarily hold at pretraining scales of hundreds of millions of images. Two later results complicate the story from opposite directions: masked pretraining recovered much of the sample efficiency for plain ViTs without any convolution, and ConvNeXt showed that a pure convolutional network modernised with the same training recipe matched hierarchical Transformers outright — which suggests a good deal of the credit assigned to attention-plus-convolution belonged to the recipe.

refs.t: CvT: Introducing Convolutions to Vision Transformers

pvt.lead: PVT made the vision Transformer usable as a detection and segmentation backbone by giving it what ViT structurally lacked: a feature pyramid. Four stages at strides 4, 8, 16 and 32 replace ViT's single stride-16 column, and spatial-reduction attention keeps the cost of the high-resolution early stages affordable by shrinking keys and values before the score matrix is formed.

blocks.h: Why ViT could not do detection
blocks.b:
ViT is columnar by construction. One patch embedding at stride 16, then a stack of identical blocks at a single resolution, then a class token. Detectors and segmenters are built on the opposite assumption — an FPN or a segmentation head wants feature maps at several strides, typically 4 through 32, because objects appear at many sizes and localisation needs resolution that classification does not.

Worse, the obvious fix is barred by cost. A stride-4 tokenisation of a $224\times224$ image gives over three thousand tokens, and self-attention is quadratic in that count, so the very stage a dense-prediction backbone needs most is the one plain attention cannot afford. In practice this meant vision Transformers were classification models and CNN backbones still owned COCO.

PVT stacks four stages, each beginning with its own patch embedding applied to the previous stage's output map. Patch size 4 at the input and 2 thereafter gives strides 4, 8, 16 and 32, with channel width increasing as resolution falls. Each stage produces a feature map of the shape a CNN backbone would produce, so PVT drops into RetinaNet, Mask R-CNN or Semantic FPN in place of a ResNet with no change to the head. The class token is confined to the last stage, since the intermediate stages exist to emit maps rather than a global vector. Position embeddings are per-stage and interpolated when the input resolution changes, as it does between classification pretraining and detection fine-tuning.

To make the early stages affordable, attention keeps every query but reduces the keys and values. Before projection, the $HW \times C$ token sequence is reshaped so that each $R\times R$ spatial block becomes one token of $R^2C$ channels, then projected back to $C$:

$$\mathrm{SR}(x) = \mathrm{Norm}\!\left(\mathrm{Reshape}(x, R)\,W_S\right)$$

Attention then runs between $HW$ queries and $HW/R^2$ key–value pairs, so the cost falls from $O((HW)^2C)$ to $O((HW)^2C/R^2)$. The reduction ratio is largest where the map is largest — $8, 4, 2, 1$ across the four stages — so the cost per stage is roughly balanced. Every query still attends globally, over the whole image rather than a local window; what is coarsened is the resolution at which the rest of the image is seen.

PVT-Small substituted for ResNet-50 in RetinaNet improved COCO box AP by around four points, and similar gains held across detection and segmentation heads. That was the point being argued: the gap between Transformers and CNNs on dense prediction had been an interface problem, not evidence that global attention was unsuited to localisation. Together with Swin, published within weeks, it established the hierarchical vision Transformer as the default backbone shape for the next two years, and it made the choice of how to cheapen attention — global-but-coarsened here, exact-but-windowed in Swin — the axis along which the following work was organised.

Collapsing an $R\times R$ block into a single key — by reshape and learned projection, not by pooling, but a compression either way — still gives up much of the fine detail that stride-4 features were introduced to preserve; small objects and thin boundaries are where the loss shows. The complexity is also only reduced, not changed in kind — still quadratic in $HW$, with a smaller constant, so genuinely high-resolution input remains expensive. Non-overlapping patch embedding leaves a discontinuity at every patch boundary, and the interpolated fixed-size position embeddings sit awkwardly with the variable input sizes detection training uses. PVTv2 answered all three: pooling to a fixed spatial size for linear complexity, overlapping patch embedding, and a depthwise convolution in the feed-forward network that supplies position so the embedding table can go.

refs.t: Pyramid Vision Transformer: A Versatile Backbone for Dense Prediction without Convolutions

pvt2.lead: PVT-v2 is three targeted repairs to PVT: overlapping patch embedding, so tokens do not break local continuity at patch boundaries; linear spatial-reduction attention, which pools keys and values to a fixed $7\times7$ grid and so makes attention linear rather than quadratic in the number of pixels; and a depthwise convolution inside the feed-forward network, which supplies position information and lets the position embedding be deleted outright.

blocks.b:
PVT's patch embeddings are non-overlapping projections, so a token is a function of one disjoint tile and the model has no direct way to represent structure that straddles a boundary — a real cost for a backbone whose job is delineating object edges.

Its spatial-reduction attention lowers the constant but keeps the quadratic form: with a fixed reduction ratio $R$ per stage, cost still grows as $(HW)^2$, so the high-resolution inputs detection actually uses stay expensive.

And position is carried by a fixed-size learned table that must be interpolated whenever the input resolution changes. Detection and segmentation change it constantly — multi-scale training, arbitrary aspect ratios — so the one component that cannot handle variable input sits inside a backbone designed for tasks that demand it.

Linear SRA replaces the reduction-ratio reshape with adaptive average pooling to a fixed $P\times P$ spatial size, $P = 7$, before the key and value projections. Every query still attends to a global summary of the image, but that summary has $49$ entries regardless of input size, so the cost is $O(HW P^2 C)$ — **linear in the number of pixels, with the constant fixed by $P$ rather than by the resolution**. The practical difference from PVT is largest exactly where it was needed: at stride 4 on a large input, where a fixed ratio still leaves thousands of keys. The trade is that the global context every query sees is now very coarse; the paper's evidence that this is acceptable is empirical, and it holds because the pyramid's later stages recover context at higher fidelity on smaller maps.

blocks.h: Overlapping patches and a convolution in the MLP
blocks.b: The patch embedding becomes a zero-padded convolution with kernel larger than stride, so adjacent tokens share input pixels and local continuity survives the tokenisation. Inside each block, a $3\times3$ depthwise convolution with zero padding is inserted between the two linear layers of the feed-forward network. It is cheap, it adds local mixing that attention over a pooled summary cannot provide, and — the reason it is there — the zero padding leaks absolute position, a property of padded convolutions that had been analysed shortly before. With position available from the convolution at every block, the position embedding table is removed, and the backbone accepts any input resolution without interpolation.

PVT-v2 improved on PVT across the board — around 82% ImageNet top-1 at roughly 25M parameters for the mid-sized variant, and consistent gains on COCO detection and ADE20K segmentation with unchanged heads — and the linear-SRA variants, reported separately as "-Li", held that accuracy while cutting cost at high resolution. It was widely adopted as a backbone precisely because it was undemanding: a linear-cost, resolution-agnostic drop-in for ResNet. Its unresolved tension is the one CvT shares. Position now comes from padding, local mixing from depthwise convolution, and downsampling from strided convolution, so what remains distinctly Transformer-like is a globally pooled attention over 49 summary vectors. ViTDet then argued from the other side that the hierarchy could be dispensed with altogether, given a plain ViT and a simple pyramid built after the fact.

refs.t: PVT v2: Improved Baselines with Pyramid Vision Transformer

crossvit.lead: CrossViT runs two Transformer branches over the same image at two patch sizes and lets them exchange information through cross-attention on their class tokens alone. The point of the restriction is cost: because only one token per branch acts as a query, the fusion is linear in sequence length rather than quadratic, so multi-scale reasoning is added to a ViT for a small fraction of what full cross-branch attention would cost.

blocks.h: One patch size is one guess
blocks.b:
A ViT commits to a patch size once and lives with it. At $16\times16$ the token count is manageable and fine structure is smoothed away inside each patch; at $8\times8$ the model sees more, and the token count quadruples, so attention costs sixteen times as much. Accuracy does improve with smaller patches, which is the awkward part — the architecture has a knob that helps when turned and cannot afford to be turned.

A convolutional network never faces this choice. Its pyramid produces several scales as a by-product of pooling, and a detector reads whichever it needs. ViT has exactly one scale from the first layer to the last, so the granularity of what it can represent is fixed before any learning happens.

CrossViT tokenises the image twice, with patch sizes 12 and 16 in every released variant — an (8, 16) pair was tried and came out slightly worse, the gap in granularity being too wide to fuse smoothly — and runs a separate Transformer over each, each with its own class token and position embeddings. The two branches are not symmetric. The coarse branch has few tokens, so it is given the greater depth and width; the fine branch has many tokens and is kept shallow, since its per-layer cost is far higher. Capacity is therefore allocated by what a layer costs at that granularity rather than split evenly. The branches alternate between blocks of their own processing and a fusion step, three times over, and at the end each class token goes to its own classifier head, the two predictions being averaged.

blocks.h: Fusion through the class token only
blocks.b:
At each fusion step, the class token of one branch is linearly projected into the other branch's dimension and used as the sole query in a cross-attention layer whose keys and values are that branch's patch tokens. The output is projected back and returned to its own branch as the updated class token. Since there is one query and $n$ keys, the fusion costs $O(n)$, where attending all patch tokens of one branch to all of the other would cost $O(n_1 n_2)$.

The justification is that the class token has already aggregated its branch, so it is a competent agent for the exchange. The paper compares against the alternatives — concatenating all tokens, pairwise fusion, simply summing the class tokens — and the cross-attention scheme is the most accurate of the four, far below all-attention in cost and only marginally above the two cheap heuristics, which is the substance of the claim.

blocks.h: What it showed, and what it is not
blocks.b:
Trained on ImageNet-1k alone, CrossViT improved on DeiT by a point or two at comparable FLOPs, which was enough to make the case that multi-scale tokens rather than a better training recipe could close part of the gap to CNNs. The bottleneck-token idea outlived the model: exchanging a small number of summary tokens between two streams became a standard cheap fusion primitive, notably for cross-modal encoders.

As a backbone it stopped short. Two branches at fixed, hand-chosen patch sizes are not a pyramid — there is no stride-4 map, no stride-32 map, nothing an FPN can consume — so CrossViT stayed a classification model while PVT and Swin took dense prediction. And a single class token is a narrow channel: whatever the fine branch resolves that does not survive its own pooling into one vector never reaches the coarse branch at all.

refs.t: CrossViT: Cross-Attention Multi-Scale Vision Transformer for Image Classification

resnest.lead: ResNeSt puts attention inside the convolution groups rather than around the block that contains them. A stage's channels are divided into cardinality groups in the ResNeXt manner, each group is divided again into radix splits, and a softmax across the splits decides — per channel — which split to listen to. ResNeSt-50 reported 81.1% top-1 on ImageNet at 224 pixels, well above a stock ResNet-50, and the interesting argument afterwards was how much of that came from the block and how much from the training recipe.

blocks.h: Attention was applied outside the block
blocks.b:
Squeeze-and-Excitation had already shown that a cheap global gate helps: pool the block output to one number per channel, pass it through two small fully connected layers, and rescale. But that gate acts on the block as a whole, after the branches have been merged. ResNeXt, meanwhile, had shown grouped convolution to be a cheap axis of capacity, yet its groups are summed or concatenated with equal weight — nothing lets one group defer to another. Selective Kernel Networks had bridged part of the gap by softmaxing over two branches with different kernel sizes.

The gap ResNeSt aimed at is the combination: **feature-map groups that compete for a channel's output before the merge**, rather than a single gate applied once the merge is done.

An input is split into $K$ cardinality groups, and each group into $R$ radix splits, giving $G = KR$ parallel feature maps produced by ordinary grouped convolutions. Within one cardinality group $k$, the $R$ splits are summed and globally average-pooled to a channel descriptor $s^k$, which passes through a bottlenecked two-layer transform $\mathcal{G}$. The gate is then a softmax taken across splits rather than a sigmoid taken per channel:

$a_i^{c} = \dfrac{\exp\!\left(\mathcal{G}_i^{c}(s^{k})\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{R}\exp\!\left(\mathcal{G}_j^{c}(s^{k})\right)}, \qquad V^{k} = \sum_{i=1}^{R} a_i^{k}\odot U_i^{k}$

where $U_i^k$ is the $i$-th split's feature map and $c$ indexes channels. The group outputs are concatenated and added to the shortcut, exactly as in a ResNet bottleneck.

blocks.h: Why a softmax, and why it is cheap
blocks.b:
The softmax makes the splits compete: weights within a group sum to one, so raising one split's contribution must lower another's. A per-channel sigmoid, as in SE, allows every branch to be turned up at once, which recovers a rescaling rather than a selection. At $R=1$ the softmax degenerates and the block reduces to SE applied per cardinality group, which is a useful sanity check on the ablation.

Nothing here requires a custom kernel. Laying the tensor out radix-major lets the whole thing be expressed with standard grouped convolutions, a reshape and a sum, so a ResNeSt is a drop-in backbone: the same stage counts, the same strides, the same downstream detection and segmentation heads.

As a backbone swap it moved the numbers that matter downstream — detection on COCO and semantic segmentation on ADE20K both improved over ResNet and ResNeXt at similar cost, which is the test a classification backbone actually has to pass.

The complication is that ResNeSt was trained with a heavy modern recipe — label smoothing, mixup, AutoAugment, DropBlock, cosine schedule, long training — while the ResNet numbers it was placed against were not. The 2021 study that retrained a plain ResNet-50 under a comparable procedure reached 80.4% top-1, which leaves much less room for the architectural claim. **The block was real; the margin attributed to it was not all its own.**

Split-attention costs little in FLOPs and rather more in wall-clock: the splits, pooling, softmax and weighted sum are memory-bandwidth work sitting between two convolutions, so throughput per FLOP is worse than a plain ResNet on most accelerators. That is the same tax SE pays, multiplied by radix.

More decisively, the frontier moved. Within a year the accuracy-per-compute argument on ImageNet was being won by vision transformers, by hybrid conv-attention designs, and by convolutional networks rebuilt around transformer-era training recipes and large kernels.
