Attention within convolution groups did not survive as a general primitive; the durable lesson from this line of work is that architectural comparisons are only meaningful when the training procedure is held fixed.

refs.t: ResNeSt: Split-Attention Networks
ResNet strikes back: An improved training procedure in timm

cspnet.lead: CSPNet is not a network so much as a rewiring rule for a stage. The stage's input feature map is split along channels; one half passes through the dense or residual block, the other bypasses it entirely and is concatenated at the transition. The paper reported roughly a fifth less computation at equal or better accuracy, and the pattern went on to become the standard backbone structure of the YOLO family from v4 onwards.

blocks.h: Dense connectivity pays for itself twice
blocks.b:
In a DenseNet stage each layer takes the concatenation of every earlier output, $x_k = w_k * [x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}]$, so during backpropagation the weight update of layer $k$ is a function of the same gradient contributions that already shaped layers $1$ through $k-1$:

$w_k' = f\!\left(w_k, g_0, g_1, \dots, g_{k-1}\right)$

Different layers therefore learn from largely **duplicated gradient information**, which the authors read as capacity spent on repetition. The second cost is plainer: concatenating a growing stack at every layer means the stage's activations are read and written repeatedly, so a design that looks modest in FLOPs is expensive in memory traffic and in the peak footprint that decides the batch size you can fit.

blocks.h: Split the stage, merge at the transition
blocks.b:
The base feature map of a stage is split by channel, $x_0 \to [x_0', x_0'']$. Only $x_0''$ enters the dense or residual block; $x_0'$ is carried across the stage untouched. The block's output passes a transition convolution, is concatenated with $x_0'$, and a second transition mixes the two.

Because the two halves are never inputs to the same block, the gradients reaching them travel different paths, and the copying described above is truncated rather than merely diluted. The ordering matters: fusing after the block's own transition — fusion last — keeps the two gradient paths distinct, whereas fusing before it re-entangles them and the paper measures the accuracy cost of doing so.

blocks.h: Why a channel split is enough
blocks.b:
The change adds no parameters and no new operator; it is a slice and a concatenation. The convolutions inside the block now see half the input channels, so their cost falls quadratically in the split ratio for the transition layers and linearly elsewhere, and the peak activation footprint falls with it. That is where the measured saving comes from.

The gradient-duplication story is an argument rather than a proof — it is not accompanied by a measurement showing that the truncated paths carry demonstrably different information. What is reproducible is the trade the rewiring makes: at matched accuracy you spend less compute and less memory bandwidth, and at matched compute you can afford a wider stage. That is enough to explain why it spread.

CSPDarknet-53 became the backbone of YOLOv4, and cross-stage splits survive in the C3 and C2f blocks of the later YOLO releases; the same group's ELAN and E-ELAN in YOLOv7 generalise the idea into explicit gradient-path planning, choosing how many distinct paths a block should expose. Other pieces of the original paper — the exact fusion module proposed for detection necks — did not travel.

What remains unresolved is that the split ratio is a hand-set hyperparameter, usually a half, never searched; the design is still concatenation-heavy and therefore still bandwidth-bound on accelerators that would rather have dense matrix work; and on backbones that were not already densely connected the accuracy gain at fixed compute is small.

refs.t: CSPNet: A New Backbone that can Enhance Learning Capability of CNN

effnetv2.lead: EfficientNet-v2 answers a complaint about its predecessor: compound scaling produced models that were remarkably parameter-efficient and slow to train. The fix is threefold — put ordinary convolutions back into the early stages, put training step time into the search objective itself, and grow the image size during training while ramping regularisation along with it.

blocks.b:
The v1 family scaled depth, width and resolution together by a single coefficient, and by B6 or B7 that meant training on very large images. Activation memory grows with resolution, so batch size has to fall, and throughput falls with it — the largest models were memory-bound before they were compute-bound.

Second, depthwise convolutions have few FLOPs per byte moved and no fused kernel on most accelerators. In the early stages, where resolution is high and channel counts low, an MBConv spends its time waiting on memory rather than on arithmetic.

Third, scaling every stage by the same rule is arbitrary. Nothing in the compound-scaling derivation says that the last stage and the first should be deepened at the same rate.

blocks.h: Fused-MBConv, and where to put it
blocks.b:
A Fused-MBConv replaces the $1\times1$ expansion followed by a $3\times3$ depthwise convolution with a single $3\times3$ dense convolution at the expansion ratio. It has more parameters and more FLOPs than the block it replaces and is nevertheless faster in the early stages, because a dense convolution over few channels at high resolution keeps the multiply-accumulate units busy while a depthwise one does not.

Using it everywhere loses that trade: in the deep, wide, low-resolution stages the FLOP increase dominates. Rather than guess the crossover, v2 hands it to a **training-aware neural architecture search** whose reward multiplies validation accuracy by decreasing functions of measured training step time and parameter count, so a block that is fast in theory and slow on the machine cannot win.

Training on small images first and enlarging them later is an old throughput trick, and it had a known cost: accuracy came out slightly below a fixed-size run. The paper's diagnosis is that regularisation was held constant while image size was not. A small crop is already an aggressive augmentation, so the same dropout rate and the same RandAugment magnitude that suit a $300$-pixel image over-regularise a $128$-pixel one.

So v2 ramps them together: as the image grows through training, dropout, mixup and augmentation magnitude grow with it. The schedule then gives the speed-up without the accuracy penalty, and the paper shows it helping plain ResNets and the original EfficientNets too, which suggests it is a property of the training procedure rather than of these particular blocks.

blocks.h: What changed, and what it did not fix
blocks.b:
The family trains several times faster than the models it was measured against at comparable or better accuracy, and the large variant pretrained on ImageNet-21k reached 87.3% top-1 on ImageNet-1k, ahead of a comparable ViT-L while using far less training time on the same hardware. The scaling rule also became non-uniform: a cap on maximum image size, and extra layers added preferentially to the later stages.

What it left is a purely convolutional design whose search space is hand-restricted and whose search is expensive to repeat. Within months the accuracy-per-training-cost frontier moved to conv-attention hybrids — CoAtNet, from the same authors — and to transformers trained with better recipes. The progressive schedule, too, is a set of knobs that must be retuned per dataset and budget.

refs.t: EfficientNetV2: Smaller Models and Faster Training

mbv4.lead: MobileNet-v4 is a response to fragmentation. MobileNet-v3 had been searched against the latency of one target, a phone CPU, and by 2024 "mobile" meant CPUs, mobile GPUs, DSPs, Apple's Neural Engine and EdgeTPUs, each with a different balance of compute to bandwidth. The answer is a block family general enough that one search can land on the Pareto front of all of them at once.

blocks.h: Optimal for one accelerator is not optimal for five
blocks.b:
Whether a block is fast is decided by where its operational intensity — arithmetic per byte of memory traffic — sits relative to the device's ridge point, the intensity above which a chip becomes compute-bound. A depthwise convolution has very low intensity: a handful of multiplies per weight fetched. On a CPU with generous cache relative to its arithmetic throughput that is tolerable; on an EdgeTPU with a large multiply-accumulate array it wastes most of the machine, and some fixed-function NPUs support grouped convolution poorly or not at all.

A front searched against a single device therefore does not transfer. MobileNet-v4 evaluates candidates against a spread of ridge points rather than one measured latency, and looks for designs that are acceptable across the range instead of optimal at one point on it.

The UIB is an inverted bottleneck with two optional depthwise convolutions: one before the $1\times1$ expansion and one between the expansion and the projection. Turning them on and off recovers four known blocks from one template — the classic inverted bottleneck with only the middle depthwise, a ConvNeXt-style block with the depthwise first, a plain feed-forward block with neither, and a new Extra-DW variant with both, which buys extra receptive field and spatial mixing at low cost.

Each block's configuration, kernel size and expansion ratio are left to the search. The practical payoff is narrow but real: a backend team optimises **one kernel family** rather than several, and the search can trade spatial mixing against cost without leaving the family.

The hybrid variants add Mobile MQA, a multi-query attention block: all query heads share a single key head and a single value head. At batch size one — the mobile case — attention is bound by the memory traffic of moving keys and values, not by its FLOPs, so collapsing them raises arithmetic intensity where it actually binds. The block additionally downsamples keys and values spatially, since neighbouring positions at these resolutions are highly redundant, and it is placed only in the last stages where the feature map is small enough to make quadratic cost irrelevant.

The paper reports upwards of a 39% inference speed-up over standard multi-head self-attention on mobile accelerators at comparable quality, which is what makes attention affordable on this class of device at all.

blocks.h: The result, and the caveat under it
blocks.b:
The family is reported Pareto-optimal across the tested CPUs, GPUs, DSPs and EdgeTPUs rather than on any one of them, and the largest hybrid variant reaches roughly 87% ImageNet top-1 at a few milliseconds on a Pixel EdgeTPU — with a distillation recipe doing part of that work.

That is also the caveat. A good share of the accuracy comes from the distillation and data-mixing procedure rather than from the block, and the block's universality is measured against a snapshot of hardware chosen largely from one vendor's ecosystem. Integer-only NPUs still handle attention awkwardly, quantisation behaviour of the hybrid variants is a separate problem, and the next generation of accelerators will move the ridge points the search was tuned against.

refs.t: MobileNetV4: Universal Models for the Mobile Ecosystem

yolov2.lead: YOLOv2 kept the single-pass premise of the original and rebuilt almost everything around it in pursuit of recall: batch normalisation throughout, a classifier fine-tuned at detection resolution, and anchor boxes whose shapes were clustered from the training data rather than guessed. On PASCAL VOC 2007 it reported 76.8 mAP at 67 frames per second, and 78.6 at a larger input — the same weights, run at a different size.

blocks.h: What v1 could not recover from
blocks.b:
The original YOLO divided the image into a $7\times7$ grid and let each cell predict two boxes and one class distribution: 98 boxes for the entire image, with coordinates regressed directly by fully connected layers. Two failure modes followed. Localisation error was high compared with Fast R-CNN, and recall was low compared with region-proposal detectors.

Of the two, recall is the one that cannot be repaired downstream. A better classifier can fix a mislabelled box and better regression can tighten a loose one, but **an object for which no box was ever emitted is simply absent from the output**. One class distribution per cell also made two objects of different classes in the same cell unrepresentable, which is exactly the crowded case that matters.

blocks.h: Anchors, and clustering rather than guessing
blocks.b:
The fully connected layers are removed and predictions are made convolutionally at every cell of a $13\times13$ map — the input is set to 416 rather than 448 so that the grid is odd and a single central cell exists, since large objects tend to be centred. Each cell predicts several boxes as offsets from priors, taking the box count from 98 to over a thousand, and each box now carries its own class distribution. Recall rose from 81% to 88% while mAP dipped slightly, a trade the remaining changes then recovered.

The priors themselves come from $k$-means over the training boxes, using $d(\mathrm{box}, \mathrm{centroid}) = 1 - \mathrm{IoU}$ as the distance, because Euclidean distance on box dimensions gives large boxes disproportionate influence. Five clusters sat at the elbow of the average-IoU curve.

blocks.h: Constraining where a box may go
blocks.b:
A region proposal network predicts centres as $x = t_x w_a + x_a$, unbounded, so any anchor can in principle claim any part of the image and training is unstable until the offsets settle. YOLOv2 instead ties each prediction to the cell that made it:

$b_x = \sigma(t_x) + c_x, \quad b_y = \sigma(t_y) + c_y, \quad b_w = p_w e^{t_w}, \quad b_h = p_h e^{t_h}$

with $(c_x, c_y)$ the cell's corner, $(p_w, p_h)$ the prior's dimensions, and confidence itself squashed as $\sigma(t_o)$. A passthrough layer folds the earlier $26\times26$ features into the $13\times13$ map by stacking them along channels, restoring fine detail lost to stride. Darknet-19 replaces VGG-16 at roughly a fifth of its convolutional cost.

Because the network is fully convolutional, its input size is a runtime choice. Training resizes the input every ten batches across a range from 320 to 608 pixels, so one set of weights spans a speed-accuracy curve that would otherwise require separate models — an unusually cheap piece of engineering that later detectors inherited.

The companion result, YOLO9000, trains jointly on detection and ImageNet classification over a WordNet-derived label hierarchy, with softmaxes taken over sibling sets and only the classification terms backpropagated for classification images, giving detection over 9000 categories.

What remained: one prediction scale, so small and clustered objects stayed weak, and anchors that are dataset-specific hyperparameters. YOLOv3 answered with three scales and independent logistic class predictions; the anchor-free detectors removed the priors entirely.

refs.t: YOLO9000: Better, Faster, Stronger

effdet.lead: EfficientDet takes seriously two parts of a detector that had been scaled by hand: how features from different pyramid levels should be combined, and how backbone, neck, head and input resolution should grow relative to each other. BiFPN gives each fusion input a learned weight and repeats a bidirectional path as a stackable layer; compound scaling then grows the whole detector from a single coefficient, producing a family from D0 to D7 spanning more than two orders of magnitude of compute — roughly 2.5B FLOPs to over 300B.

blocks.b:
A feature pyramid network fuses scales top-down: upsample the coarser map, add it to the finer one, convolve. The addition treats its inputs as equal contributors even though one has been upsampled by a factor of two or four from a map of much lower resolution and the other has not. There is no reason to expect equal usefulness, and no mechanism to discover otherwise.

PANet added a bottom-up path and did measurably better at higher cost. NAS-FPN searched the topology directly, at thousands of GPU-hours, and returned an irregular graph that is difficult to interpret or to scale. **Both changed the wiring; neither questioned the sum.**

blocks.h: BiFPN: three edits and a weighting
blocks.b:
First, nodes with a single input edge are deleted — a node that fuses nothing contributes little to a fusion network. Second, an extra skip edge runs from the original input to the output node at the same level, adding features at no meaningful cost. Third, one top-down plus bottom-up pass is treated as a layer and repeated.

Each fusion is then weighted, with weights kept non-negative by a ReLU and normalised:

$O = \sum_{i} \frac{w_i}{\epsilon + \sum_{j} w_j} \cdot I_i$

where $I_i$ are the resized inputs, $w_i$ scalar learned weights, and $\epsilon$ a small constant guarding the division. A softmax over the weights gave equivalent accuracy and ran noticeably slower on GPU, so the cheaper normalised form was kept. Fusion nodes use depthwise separable convolutions with batch normalisation.

blocks.h: One coefficient for the whole detector
blocks.b:
EfficientNet's compound scaling covered a classifier. A detector has three more parts, and practice had been to enlarge the backbone and leave the neck and head as they were, which puts a small fusion network behind a large feature extractor.

EfficientDet ties them: the backbone steps through EfficientNet-B0 to B6, the BiFPN width grows as $64 \cdot 1.35^{\phi}$ and its depth as $3 + \phi$, the box and class heads deepen as $3 + \lfloor \phi/3 \rfloor$, and the input resolution as $512 + 128\phi$. Only the width ratio was found by grid search; the rest are linear rules. The result is that one design decision produces a family covering mobile-scale to server-scale rather than seven separately tuned detectors.

blocks.h: Anchors and NMS were left alone
blocks.b:
As first reported, the largest variant reached 52.2 AP on COCO test-dev with about 52M parameters and far fewer FLOPs than the previous best detector, and later releases pushed higher. But depthwise-heavy convolutions at high resolution use hardware poorly, so measured latency lagged what the FLOP counts implied; the YOLO line, with plainer convolutions and path-aggregation necks, kept winning on real throughput.

Structurally, everything before the neck's outputs was rethought and everything after was not. Anchors remain, with hand-set scales and aspect ratios per level, alongside the focal loss inherited from RetinaNet. Inference still ends in non-maximum suppression: a non-differentiable postprocess whose IoU threshold trades duplicate boxes against genuinely overlapping objects. DETR removed both that same year, at the cost of a far longer training schedule.

refs.t: EfficientDet: Scalable and Efficient Object Detection

maskformer.lead: MaskFormer's claim is in its title: per-pixel classification is not all you need for semantic segmentation. Rather than assigning every pixel one of $K$ class labels, it predicts a fixed set of $N$ binary masks, each carrying a single class label, and shows that this one formulation — with one architecture and one loss — covers semantic and panoptic segmentation alike, leaving instance segmentation to the same idea a few months later.

blocks.h: Two tasks that had grown apart
blocks.b:
Since the fully convolutional network, semantic segmentation had meant a softmax over classes at every pixel. Instance segmentation cannot be written that way at all: two people in one image share a label, so the pixel-wise formulation has no way to separate them. Mask R-CNN therefore detects boxes first and segments within each, which is mask classification in all but name. Panoptic segmentation, wanting both, was typically built as two heads with a merging heuristic to reconcile their disagreements.

The per-pixel view has a second awkwardness. Its output dimensionality is tied to $K$, and each pixel is classified independently of any notion of the region it belongs to — so as the label set grows, the task grows harder in a way that has little to do with segmentation.

A backbone feeds two branches. A pixel decoder upsamples to per-pixel embeddings $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{pixel}}$ at high resolution. A transformer decoder takes $N$ learned queries and cross-attends to the backbone features, producing $N$ per-segment embeddings. A linear layer turns each into a distribution over $K+1$ classes, the extra one being "no object"; a small MLP turns each into a mask embedding $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mask}}^{i}$. The mask itself is then just a dot product per pixel:

$m_i = \mathrm{sigmoid}\!\left(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mask}}^{i\top}\,\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{pixel}}\right)$

$N$ is fixed — 100 in the standard configuration — and **entirely independent of the number of classes**, so the model's output capacity is a count of regions rather than a count of labels.

blocks.h: Matching in training, marginalising at inference
blocks.b:
Since the $N$ predictions are an unordered set, training uses bipartite matching, as in DETR: a Hungarian assignment pairs predictions with ground-truth segments, matched pairs receive a classification loss plus a mask loss combining focal and dice terms, and unmatched predictions are pushed towards the no-object class.

Inference differs only in the readout. For panoptic output each pixel is assigned to the highest-scoring query-class pair, and low-confidence or tiny segments are filtered. For a semantic map the queries are marginalised away,

$\arg\max_{c}\ \sum_{i=1}^{N} p_i(c)\, m_i[h,w]$

with $p_i(c)$ the $i$-th query's probability for class $c$. The same weights serve both tasks; only the final aggregation changes.

blocks.h: Where the margin appears, and what stayed slow
blocks.b:
The evidence for the claim is a pattern rather than a single number. On Cityscapes, with 19 classes, mask classification roughly matches a strong per-pixel baseline. On ADE20K with 150 classes and COCO-Stuff with 171 the gap opens and keeps widening — precisely what one expects if the benefit is decoupling output count from label count. A single Swin-based model was simultaneously competitive on semantic and panoptic benchmarks that had previously required different architectures.

The costs are inherited from DETR: set matching converges slowly, requiring long schedules, and cross-attention is global over a coarse feature map, so small objects are poorly served while finer features are unaffordable at quadratic cost. Mask2Former answered directly — cross-attention restricted to each query's predicted foreground, multi-scale features fed to successive decoder layers, and mask loss computed on sampled points.

refs.t: Per-Pixel Classification is Not All You Need for Semantic Segmentation
Masked-attention Mask Transformer for Universal Image Segmentation

neocog.lead: The Neocognitron is the convolutional network as it existed before backpropagation: a deep hierarchy of alternating feature-extracting and position-tolerating layers, with weights shared across each layer's spatial extent. Fukushima built it directly from Hubel and Wiesel's account of simple and complex cells, and every structural element of a modern CNN is already present — everything except the learning rule.

blocks.h: What the Cognitron could not do
blocks.b:
Fukushima's earlier Cognitron, like the perceptron before it, learned templates tied to absolute position: shift the input pattern by a few cells and the response collapsed. The standard remedy was to normalise position before recognition, centring and size-normalising each character, which works on cleanly segmented print and fails the moment position must be discovered rather than assumed.

Hubel and Wiesel had described two families of cell in the cat's visual cortex: simple cells firing for an oriented edge at one retinal location, and complex cells firing for the same edge anywhere in a larger region. Fukushima's wager was that alternating those two types would build tolerance **gradually, a little at each stage**, instead of demanding all of it from a single final layer.

S-layers and C-layers alternate. An S-cell takes a modifiable local receptive field over the layer below, and all S-cells in one cell-plane share a single set of afferent weights, so the plane computes one feature at every position:

$u_S(n) = \varphi\!\left(\sum_{v \in A} a(v)\, u_C(n+v) \; - \; b\, c(n)\right)$

Here $n$ indexes position, $A$ is the receptive field, $a$ the shared excitatory weights, and $c(n)$ an inhibitory cell measuring local activity, so the cell reports a contrast rather than an absolute amount. Fukushima's own form is divisive rather than subtractive, and his $\varphi$ is the half-wave rectifier later renamed ReLU. Because $a$ does not depend on $n$, translating the input translates the response. A C-cell then pools over a small neighbourhood of one S-plane, converting that equivariance into tolerance.

Training is unsupervised and strictly local. Cells are grouped into columns covering the same retinal position; when a pattern is presented, the most strongly responding S-cell in a column is taken as the representative for its plane, its afferent weights are reinforced in proportion to the activity that produced the response, and every other cell in the plane copies them. Weight sharing is maintained by the learning rule rather than imposed as a constraint on a gradient.

There is no target, no error, and no communication downward between layers. Each stage learns whatever recurs in the output of the stage beneath it. That is why the features are what they are, and why they cannot be shaped by the task the network is eventually asked to perform.

Demonstrated in 1980 on a handful of hand-drawn numerals, the network recognised patterns that were shifted or distorted in shape and size, and the tolerance came from the architecture rather than from a large set of augmented training examples. Local receptive fields, shared weights, alternating convolution and subsampling, receptive fields widening with depth — the whole skeleton of LeNet is here in 1980.

What is absent is credit assignment. Without a global error signal there is no way to trade a decision made early against a mistake made late, so features are competitive winners rather than discriminative ones, and each added stage buys less than it should. Backpropagation supplied exactly that missing piece, and LeCun's convolutional work through the following two decades amounts to keeping Fukushima's architecture and replacing his learning rule.

lenet.lead: LeNet-5 is the demonstration that a convolutional network trained end to end by gradient descent beats a hand-built feature pipeline on a task someone was paying for. It reads $32\times32$ grey images through alternating convolution and subsampling layers, reaches under one per cent error on MNIST, and in commercial descendants was reading a substantial share of the cheques processed in the United States by the late 1990s.

blocks.b:
Character recognition in the early 1990s was a pipeline: segment the image, compute hand-designed descriptors — moments, skeletons, structural primitives, zoning histograms — and hand the vector to a classifier. Each stage was tuned separately against its own proxy objective, and the descriptors encoded a designer's guess about what distinguishes a 3 from an 8.

A fully connected network on raw pixels avoids the guessing but throws away the two-dimensional topology of the image, needs a parameter for every pixel-unit pair, and has to learn independently at every location that a stroke is a stroke. LeCun's 1989 work on handwritten postal codes had already shown that backpropagation through **shared-weight local connections** removed all three problems at once. LeNet-5 is that idea in mature form.

C1 applies six $5\times5$ kernels to produce six $28\times28$ feature maps; S2 subsamples $2\times2$ with a trainable coefficient and bias followed by a squashing nonlinearity — an averaging pool, not the max pooling that came later. C3's sixteen maps are wired to S2 through a hand-specified sparse table so that different maps see different subsets, breaking symmetry and holding down connections. S4 subsamples again; C5's $5\times5$ kernels span the whole remaining field, so it is fully connected in effect while stated as a convolution; F6 has 84 units. The ten outputs are radial basis units,

$y_i = \sum_j (x_j - w_{ij})^2$

whose fixed centres are $7\times12$ bitmaps of stylised characters, so F6 is trained to draw a picture of the class rather than to fire one hot unit. About sixty thousand parameters in total, trained with a stochastic diagonal approximation to Newton's method.

Most of the 1998 paper is not about LeNet-5. It is about graph transformer networks: training an entire document-reading system — field location, heuristic over-segmentation, character recognition, language model — as one differentiable object, so that the segmenter is trained by the recognition error it causes rather than against a separate hand-labelled criterion. Candidate segmentations form a graph, scores propagate along it, and gradients flow back through the whole structure with a discriminative loss defined at the string level.

This is end-to-end learning of a pipeline, argued and deployed twenty years before the phrase became standard. The recogniser was the reusable part; the training philosophy was the more general claim, and the one the field took much longer to accept.

The architecture worked, was deployed at industrial scale, and was largely set aside for a decade. The reasons were not architectural. Labelled sets at the scale of ImageNet did not exist, and a convolutional net with millions of parameters on a few thousand examples memorises. General-purpose GPU compute did not exist. Saturating sigmoids made deep stacks slow and initialisation-sensitive. Meanwhile kernel methods offered convex training, clean generalisation bounds, and competitive accuracy on the benchmarks then in use.

Everything AlexNet added fourteen years later — rectifiers, dropout, aggressive augmentation, two GPUs, a thousand-class dataset — addresses one of those constraints. The layer stack it trained was recognisably LeNet, widened.

alexnet.lead: AlexNet settled an open empirical question: convolutional networks had not failed on natural images, they had never been given enough data or compute. Eight learned layers trained on ImageNet across two GPUs took the ILSVRC-2012 top-5 error to 15.3% — an average over seven such networks, with a single model at 18.2% on the validation set — against 26.2% for the runner-up, and the gap was large enough that the hand-engineered vision pipeline was abandoned within about a year.

blocks.b:
State-of-the-art recognition in 2012 meant dense SIFT or HOG descriptors, quantised into a codebook or aggregated into Fisher vectors, spatially pooled, and fed to a linear SVM. Only the last stage learned anything, and the representation was fixed by hand before the labels were consulted.

Convolutional networks had been tried on natural images and had not been competitive, which was widely read as evidence that learned features did not scale beyond digits. ImageNet removed the most plausible alternative explanation: roughly 1.2 million labelled training images across a thousand classes, with fine-grained categories that a bag of quantised gradients handles badly. What remained was the compute to fit a large network to it, and that is what the paper supplied.

The network takes $224\times224$ crops through an $11\times11$ stride-4 convolution, a $5\times5$ layer, three $3\times3$ layers with overlapping $3\times3$ stride-2 max pooling, then two 4096-unit fully connected layers and a 1000-way softmax — 60 million parameters and about 650,000 units.

It is split across two GTX 580s with 3 GB each because it did not fit on one card, and the halves exchange activations only at particular layers. That constraint is **grouped convolution invented as a memory workaround**, and it was later adopted deliberately by ResNeXt and by the depthwise designs. Training ran for several days with momentum SGD and weight decay, and the paper notes the decay reduced training error rather than merely regularising.

The nonlinearity is $f(x) = \max(0, x)$. A sigmoid or tanh unit has near-zero derivative once saturated, so most of a deep network's gradient budget is spent on units that have already committed; the rectifier passes gradient unattenuated on its active side however large the input. The paper reports reaching a fixed training-error threshold on CIFAR-10 several times faster than the tanh equivalent, and that speed is what made eight layers affordable rather than merely possible.

Dropout at 0.5 is applied to the two fully connected layers, where almost all 60 million parameters sit. With random crops, horizontal flips and PCA-based colour jitter, it is what kept a model of that size from memorising 1.2 million images.

blocks.h: How much of it was guesswork
blocks.b:
The design was not derived from anything. Local response normalisation, presented as an aid to generalisation, was quietly dropped by later work that found no reliable benefit. The $11\times11$ stride-4 first layer was chosen for cost and turned out to be too coarse, which ZFNet showed the following year by projecting the features back to pixels. The two 4096-unit layers hold the overwhelming majority of the parameters for a modest share of the computation, an imbalance GoogLeNet removed with global average pooling and VGG did not.

No principle governed depth, width or kernel size. VGG's controlled depth study, GoogLeNet's compute-aware module and, soon after, batch normalisation were direct responses to exactly that.

refs.t: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

zfnet.lead: ZFNet is what happens when someone builds an instrument before building a model. Zeiler and Fergus attached a reverse pathway to a trained AlexNet that projects any single activation back into pixel space, looked at what the layers had actually learned, found two specific pathologies in the first two layers, and fixed them — winning ILSVRC-2013 with an architecture that differs from AlexNet only in kernel size, stride and width.

blocks.h: Tuning a network you cannot see
blocks.b:
After 2012 the recipe worked and nobody could say why. Architecture search meant changing a hyperparameter, retraining for days on ImageNet, and reading a single validation number — a search over a large discrete space guided by one scalar per experiment, with no signal about which layer was at fault.

The diagnostic tools available were weak. First-layer filters can be displayed directly as images, but that stops at layer one; beyond it, people showed the input patches that maximally activated a unit, which reveals which images excite a unit without saying **which structure inside those patches** is responsible. The gap between "this unit likes dogs" and "this unit responds to a particular texture at a particular scale" is where the tuning decisions live.

The deconvnet inverts the forward pass approximately, one stage at a time. Max pooling is not invertible, so the forward pass records switches — the argmax location within each pooling region — and unpooling places the value back at the recorded location, leaving the rest zero. The rectifier is inverted by another rectifier, keeping the reconstruction in the positive regime the network itself uses. The convolution is inverted by convolving with a transposed, flipped copy of the same learned filters.

To examine one unit, run an image forward, keep a single activation in the chosen layer, zero everything else in that layer, and project down. The result is a pixel-space picture of what that unit responded to in that image. Occlusion tests complement it: slide a grey square over the input and plot the drop in class probability.

The first-layer filters of AlexNet were dominated by very high and very low frequencies with little coverage in between, and the second-layer reconstructions showed aliasing artefacts attributable to the stride-4 subsampling. Both are concrete, both are fixable: reduce the first layer to $7\times7$ with stride 2 and widen the middle convolutional layers. The occlusion maps confirmed something else the community had assumed rather than checked — the classifier's confidence tracks the object, not correlated context.

The same paper made the transfer case explicitly. Truncate the network at various depths, retrain only a classifier on Caltech-101 and Caltech-256, and the ImageNet-trained features beat the best hand-crafted results by a wide margin. Pretrain-then-fine-tune became standard practice from roughly this point.

Nothing new is proposed. The contribution is a method plus two tuned hyperparameters, which is why ZFNet sits in the lineage as a hinge rather than a branch: VGG and GoogLeNet, arriving the next year, changed the structure itself.

The method also has a limit that took the field some years to state. A deconvnet projection is conditioned on the switch settings of one particular input, so it shows what a unit responded to in that image, not what the unit computes in general, and the reverse path is an approximation rather than an inverse. Gradient saliency, guided backprop, class activation mapping and optimisation-based feature visualisation all followed; later sanity checks found some of them insensitive to randomising the model's own weights, which is a warning about the whole genre.

vgg.lead: VGG is a controlled experiment rather than an invention. Simonyan and Zisserman fixed every architectural choice except one — $3\times3$ kernels, stride 1, $2\times2$ pooling, widths doubling after each pool — and varied only the number of weight layers from 11 to 19, showing that accuracy improved with depth alone. The uniformity made it the default backbone for years, and its parameter count made it the thing everyone next tried to avoid.

blocks.b:
AlexNet, ZFNet and OverFeat differed simultaneously in first-layer kernel size, stride, width, number of layers and normalisation scheme, so their score differences licensed no conclusion about any single factor. The community had strong opinions about kernel size and depth and no clean evidence for either.

VGG's design is chosen to make the comparison legible. Every convolution is $3\times3$ with stride 1 and padding 1, so spatial resolution is unchanged by convolution and falls only at the pooling layers; channels double from 64 to 512 as resolution halves, holding roughly constant computation per stage. Configurations A through E share this skeleton exactly and differ only in how many convolutions sit in each stage. **Depth is the only free variable.**

blocks.h: Three small kernels for one large
blocks.b:
A stack of three $3\times3$ convolutions has the same $7\times7$ effective receptive field as one $7\times7$ convolution. With $C$ channels in and out, the stack costs

$3(3^2 C^2) = 27C^2 \quad\text{against}\quad 7^2 C^2 = 49C^2$

parameters — about 45% fewer — and interposes three rectifiers instead of one, so the composite filter is nonlinear where the single large kernel is not.

There is a regularisation reading as well: the factorisation restricts the $7\times7$ filter to those expressible as a composition of small ones, a prior that turned out to cost nothing measurable. Configuration C adds $1\times1$ convolutions to test extra nonlinearity without changing the receptive field, and they help less than the extra $3\times3$ layers of configuration D.

There was no batch normalisation. Deep configurations were unstable from random initialisation, so the authors trained the 11-layer network first and used its early convolutional layers and its classifier to initialise the deeper ones — a staged bootstrap they noted after submission was avoidable with Glorot and Bengio's 2010 initialisation, and which He-style initialisation retired outright the following year.

Two further details mattered in practice. Training crops came from images rescaled to a randomly sampled size, giving scale jitter for free; and at test time the fully connected layers were re-expressed as convolutions, so the network scores an image of any size densely rather than through a fixed set of crops. VGG placed second in ILSVRC-2014 classification behind GoogLeNet and first in localisation.

VGG-16 carries about 138 million parameters, and roughly three quarters of them sit in the first fully connected layer, which flattens a $7\times7\times512$ map into 4096 units. Inference is on the order of 15 GFLOPs per $224^2$ image, several times GoogLeNet's, which reached a better score in the same competition with about a twentieth of the parameters by replacing the head with global average pooling.

The more consequential limit is that depth stopped paying. Going beyond 19 layers did not help, and this was not overfitting — deeper plain stacks became harder to optimise. Naming that failure degradation and giving it a fix is precisely what ResNet did the following year.

googlenet.lead: GoogLeNet won ILSVRC-2014 with 22 layers and roughly five million parameters — about a twelfth of AlexNet's — by refusing to spend compute uniformly. Its Inception module runs several kernel sizes in parallel and puts a $1\times1$ convolution in front of the expensive ones to cut channel depth first, an operation that has been load-bearing in almost every efficient architecture since.

blocks.b:
A convolutional layer with kernel size $k$ costs about $k^2 C_{\mathrm{in}} C_{\mathrm{out}}$ multiply-adds per spatial position, so doubling the width of two adjacent layers quadruples their cost. Adding capacity that way also adds parameters that need labels, and a large share of the resulting weights end up near zero — the capacity is spent, not used.

The paper's stated motivation was a result on approximating an optimal sparse network structure by clustering correlated units into dense sub-blocks, dressed with a Hebbian aside. The field has since treated that as loose justification for a design reached empirically. The durable argument is the arithmetic one: **compute, not parameters, was the binding constraint**, and it had to be allocated deliberately.

Rather than choose a kernel size per layer, the module applies $1\times1$, $3\times3$ and $5\times5$ convolutions and a $3\times3$ max pool to the same input in parallel and concatenates the outputs along the channel axis. The layer therefore represents several scales at once and lets training decide how much of the output width each scale earns, instead of the designer fixing it in advance.

The naive form is unaffordable. Concatenation makes output channels the sum of all branch widths, so width grows from layer to layer; the pooling branch passes its input channels through untouched and so can only add; and the $5\times5$ branch operates on that inflated input. Cost compounds across a stack of such modules within a few layers.

A $1\times1$ convolution is a learned linear map across channels at each spatial position, followed by a rectifier — a projection, not a spatial filter. Placed before the $5\times5$ branch it reduces $C_{\mathrm{in}}$ channels to $r$, changing the per-position cost from

$25\,C_{\mathrm{in}}C_{\mathrm{out}} \quad\text{to}\quad C_{\mathrm{in}}r + 25\,r\,C_{\mathrm{out}}$

which for $r \ll C_{\mathrm{in}}$ is roughly an order of magnitude cheaper. A $1\times1$ after the pooling branch caps its contribution to the concatenation the same way.

This single trick reappears as ResNet's bottleneck block, as the pointwise stage of a depthwise separable convolution, and as the reduction in every squeeze-and-excitation and channel-attention design that followed.

The classifier head is a global average pool over the final feature map into a single linear layer. VGG's parameters were mostly in its flattened fully connected layer; GoogLeNet simply does not have one, which is most of the parameter difference.

Two auxiliary classifiers hang off intermediate depths, their losses added at a reduced weight. They were presented as a way to push gradient into the middle of a network too deep to train comfortably in 2014. Later analysis found they help little early in training and act mainly as regularisers, and the argument for them faded once batch normalisation and residual connections addressed the underlying problem properly.

Every branch width in every module was chosen by hand for $224^2$ ImageNet classification, and the paper offers no rule for adapting them to another resolution, dataset or compute budget. Transferring the design meant re-tuning dozens of numbers with no gradient to guide the search.

The successors regularised exactly this. Batch normalisation removed much of the tuning fragility; Inception-v2 and v3 factorised $5\times5$ into two $3\times3$ and $n\times n$ into $1\times n$ followed by $n\times1$, replacing intuition with a stated rule; Inception-ResNet merged the module with residual connections; Xception pushed the branch structure to its separable limit. Architecture search eventually automated the branch-width choices Szegedy made by hand.

resnet.lead: ResNet identified a failure that was not overfitting and not vanishing gradients: past a certain depth, adding layers made plain networks worse on the training set. Rewriting each block to compute $\mathcal{F}(x) + x$ rather than $\mathcal{H}(x)$ removed it, allowing 152 layers at lower complexity than VGG-19 and a 3.57% top-5 ensemble error that swept every track of ILSVRC-2015.

blocks.b:
With batch normalisation and careful initialisation in place, the signal reaching early layers of a deep plain network was healthy and the networks converged — they just converged worse. A 34-layer plain stack had **higher training error** than an 18-layer one, which rules out overfitting: a model that memorises has low training error by definition.

The paper's framing makes the anomaly sharp. Take a trained shallow network and append layers initialised to the identity map. The resulting deep network computes exactly the same function, so its solution space contains the shallow solution and its achievable training error is no worse. Stochastic gradient descent nevertheless failed to find any solution that good. The obstacle was optimisation, not capacity.

Each block computes

$y = \mathcal{F}(x, \{W_i\}) + x$

where $\mathcal{F}$ is two or three convolutions with normalisation and rectifiers, and the shortcut carries $x$ unchanged. The block still expresses any target map $\mathcal{H}(x)$ by setting $\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{H} - x$, so nothing is lost; what changes is which functions are easy to reach. If the useful map for a given block is close to the identity, driving a stack of weights to zero is straightforward, whereas fitting an identity through several nonlinear layers is not.

The shortcut is parameter-free and adds no computation. Only where the block changes width or resolution does a $1\times1$ projection appear, which keeps the identity path clean nearly everywhere in the network.

Differentiating the block gives

$\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = I + \frac{\partial \mathcal{F}}{\partial x}$

so gradient reaching an early layer is never solely a product of many small Jacobians; there is always an additive term that survives. He et al.'s follow-up on identity mappings made the point sharper — moving normalisation and activation inside $\mathcal{F}$, leaving the shortcut entirely unobstructed, trains networks of over a thousand layers.

Two later readings complement this. Unravelling the network shows it behaves as an ensemble of paths of many lengths, with the short paths carrying most of the effective gradient. Loss-surface visualisations show the skip connections markedly smoothing a landscape that is chaotic without them.

Deep variants use a $1\times1$–$3\times3$–$1\times1$ bottleneck, borrowing GoogLeNet's channel reduction so that 152 layers cost less than VGG-19. The block became the default backbone across detection and segmentation for the better part of a decade, and the additive skip is now in essentially everything, the Transformer included.

The limits emerged quickly. Depth beyond a few hundred layers buys almost nothing, and Wide ResNets showed width was often the better axis. Every block recomputes features it could have reused, which DenseNet attacked with concatenation and ResNeXt with grouped transforms. And the receptive field is still local, growing only linearly with depth, so global context required dilation, then non-local blocks, and finally attention.

fcn.lead: FCN made a classification network emit a labelled image instead of a label. Reading the fully connected layers of a pretrained VGG as convolutions turns the network into a machine that consumes any input size and returns a coarse score map; a learned upsampling path and skip connections from earlier, finer layers turn that map back into pixels. It is the first end-to-end, pixels-to-pixels segmentation network, and the encoder-decoder template every later system argues with.

blocks.h: Sliding windows at the wrong price
blocks.b: Before 2015 the standard route to per-pixel labels was to classify a patch centred on each pixel — the approach that won the ISBI 2012 membrane challenge — or to classify region proposals and paste the results back, as R-CNN-derived systems did. Both are wasteful: neighbouring patches overlap almost completely, so the same convolutional features are recomputed hundreds of times, and the patch size fixes how much context any decision can use. The fully connected head made this structural rather than accidental: a layer with a fixed weight matrix demands a fixed input size, so a network trained on $224\times224$ crops could only ever be run on $224\times224$ crops.

blocks.h: A fully connected layer is a convolution
blocks.b:
The reinterpretation is arithmetic, not approximation. A layer mapping a $7\times7\times512$ activation to $4096$ outputs is a convolution with a $7\times7$ kernel and $4096$ output channels; the same numbers, reshaped. At the training crop size nothing changes. At a larger input the layer now slides, and the network returns a map of class scores rather than a vector.

What the map costs is resolution. Kernel size and stride compose down a network as

$f_{ks} \circ g_{k's'} = (f \circ g)_{k' + (k-1)s',\; ss'}$

so VGG's five poolings multiply to an **output stride of 32**: one prediction per $32\times32$ block of input.

blocks.h: Learned upsampling, and skips that add
blocks.b:
Bilinear interpolation is itself a convolution with fixed weights, so FCN implements upsampling as a backward-strided convolution initialised to bilinear and allowed to learn. Upsampling the stride-32 map alone (FCN-32s) gives predictions that are semantically right and spatially mushy.

The fix is to bring in layers that were never downsampled so far. A $1\times1$ layer scores `pool4` and `pool3` directly, and those scores are summed with the coarser prediction after $2\times$ upsampling, giving FCN-16s and FCN-8s. Note that what is fused is class scores, not features — a decision U-Net would reverse. Whole-image training proved as effective as patch sampling and much cheaper, and FCN-8s reached $62.2\%$ mean IU on PASCAL VOC 2012.

blocks.h: The detail that never came back
blocks.b: Fusing below `pool3` gave diminishing returns, and stride-8 predictions upsampled eightfold still smear object boundaries. The cause is structural: the features that carry semantics are the deep ones, and the deep ones are coarse. Three lines of work went after exactly this. Keep the resolution in the first place, by dilating filters instead of striding — DeepLab. Build a symmetric decoder that carries encoder detail forward with capacity, rather than adding scores — U-Net and SegNet. Or repair boundaries afterwards with a structured model, the fully connected CRF. A fourth limitation went unnoticed longer: an independent softmax per pixel has no concept of an object, which is what mask-classification approaches later replaced.

unet.lead: U-Net took FCN's insight and made the upsampling path a full network rather than an afterthought: a symmetric contracting and expanding pair, with the encoder's feature maps concatenated into the decoder at every resolution. Together with elastic-deformation augmentation and a loss weighted along cell borders, it won the ISBI segmentation challenges from roughly thirty annotated images, and it has outlived its own domain — the same shape carries almost every diffusion model.

blocks.b: Biomedical segmentation has two properties that general vision does not. Annotation requires an expert, so training sets are counted in tens of images rather than thousands; and the objects of interest are often many instances of one class pressed against each other, so a per-pixel class map does not separate them. The state of the art was a per-pixel patch classifier, which was slow, redundant, and forced a direct trade between the context a large patch supplies and the localisation a small one preserves. FCN had shown dense prediction could be done in one pass, but its decoder was a bilinear-initialised upsample summing coarse class scores — enough for PASCAL, not for a cell membrane one pixel wide.

The contracting path is conventional: repeated $3\times3$ unpadded convolutions with ReLU, $2\times2$ max pooling, channels doubling at each step. The expanding path mirrors it. Each stage applies a $2\times2$ up-convolution that halves the channel count, **concatenates the correspondingly cropped feature map from the contracting path**, then applies two more $3\times3$ convolutions.

Two choices matter. Concatenating whole feature maps rather than summing class scores gives the decoder the encoder's full description of local appearance, not just its verdict. And keeping a large channel count on the way up makes the decoder a network with capacity to combine that detail with context, rather than a resize operator with a bias term.

With thirty images, augmentation is not a regulariser but the main source of training signal, and the paper picks it to match the domain. Random displacements are sampled on a coarse grid and interpolated to give smooth elastic deformations of the image and its labels. Tissue genuinely does vary this way, so the invariance being taught is a true one; shift, rotation and grey-value perturbations are added on top.

A second practical device is the overlap-tile strategy. Because the convolutions are unpadded, the output is smaller than the input, and a large image is segmented in tiles whose input context overlaps, with mirroring at the image border — so no tile is ever predicted from padded zeros.

blocks.h: A loss that draws the borders
blocks.b:
Separating touching instances is handled in the objective rather than the architecture. Each pixel gets a weight in the cross-entropy,

$w(\mathbf{x}) = w_c(\mathbf{x}) + w_0 \exp\!\left(-\frac{(d_1(\mathbf{x}) + d_2(\mathbf{x}))^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$

where $w_c$ balances class frequencies, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the distances to the nearest and second-nearest cell. Pixels in the thin gap between two cells are close to both, so the exponential is near one and their weight is large — with $w_0 = 10$ and $\sigma$ a few pixels, the narrow background ridges separating cells dominate the gradient. The network is thus paid most for exactly the pixels a class-wise loss would ignore.

The receptive field is finite and the deepest layer of a U-Net is not very deep, so reasoning that needs whole-image context — which organ this is, whether a structure is plausible given the rest of the scene — is not well served. Later work added attention gates, then replaced or supplemented the encoder with a Transformer, and DeepLab-style pyramid pooling attacked the same gap from another direction. Instance separation remained a loss trick rather than a representation. The most useful correction came from nnU-Net, which found that a plain U-Net with automatically configured preprocessing, patch size and training schedule beats most architectural elaborations proposed since — the configuration, not the topology, was carrying the difference.

segnet.lead: SegNet is an encoder-decoder built to a memory budget rather than to a leaderboard. Its decoder upsamples using the max-pooling indices recorded by the matching encoder layer, so the location of each surviving activation is restored exactly while nothing but two bits per pooling window is stored. It was aimed at road-scene understanding on embedded hardware, and it made explicit a trade-off — how much encoder information a decoder needs — that later segmentation designs are all points on.

blocks.h: Scene labelling under a hardware budget
blocks.b: The target was automotive: label every pixel of a road scene, on a device, within a frame time. Judged that way the existing dense-prediction networks were awkward. FCN's decoder learns to upsample coarse class scores, and to do better it must retain encoder feature maps for the skip fusions. DeconvNet built a fully symmetric decoder but kept VGG's fully connected layers at the bottleneck — mirrored, so paid for twice — which put its parameter count at roughly $252$ million and made it hard to train end to end. Much of that cost buys resolution recovery, and resolution recovery is precisely where a scene-labelling network can be cheap, because the information needed is not the full feature map but where in each pooling window the response came from.

Max pooling already computes an argmax and then throws it away. SegNet stores it. For each $2\times2$ window the encoder records which of the four positions won — two bits — and the matching decoder stage scatters incoming values back to those positions, producing a sparse map that the following trainable convolutions densify.

The alternative upsamplers have no such knowledge. Bilinear interpolation, and a learned transposed convolution equally, spread a value over a window with no idea where inside it the evidence lay, so thin structures and boundaries drift. Reusing indices restores the *where* for free, and the encoder is VGG-16 with the fully connected layers deleted, which is where the parameter count falls from $134$M to roughly $15$M.

blocks.h: The comparison the paper actually ran
blocks.b:
The paper's more valuable contribution is its controlled study of decoder variants on the same encoder. Judged with memory unconstrained, carrying the encoder's full feature maps across and using them in the decoder — the U-Net arrangement — gives the best boundary accuracy. Index unpooling recovers most of that benefit at a small fraction of the storage, and beats bilinear upsampling clearly. FCN-style score fusion sits between.

Stated plainly: **indices are not better than features, they are cheaper**. That is an honest framing, and it is why SegNet's specific mechanism faded as memory got cheap while its finding — decoders need encoder information, and how much you give them is a dial — became standard reasoning.

An index says which pixel the activation came from and nothing about what was lost in the other three, so fine texture and the appearance detail a boundary needs must be re-synthesised by the decoder convolutions. Nor does the architecture add any global reasoning: the receptive field is VGG's, and a scene-level constraint such as road-below-sky is only learned implicitly. Pyramid pooling and atrous spatial pyramids answered the context gap, and boundary quality moved to dilated backbones with a light decoder. On the efficiency front, purpose-built real-time designs — ENet, ICNet, and the two-branch networks after them — beat SegNet on its own terms, by redesigning the encoder rather than economising in the decoder.

refs.t: SegNet: A Deep Convolutional Encoder-Decoder Architecture for Image Segmentation

deeplab.lead: DeepLab attacked dense prediction from the opposite side to the encoder-decoder family: instead of recovering resolution after destroying it, do not destroy it. Atrous convolution inserts holes between filter taps, so a network can drop its last pooling strides and keep the receptive field its pretrained weights expect, at an output stride of $8$ rather than $32$. A fully connected CRF then sharpened what remained soft, and atrous spatial pyramid pooling handled scale.

blocks.b: A classification backbone is built to discard position. Five rounds of striding shrink the map $32$-fold, and the invariance that buys is exactly what makes the features good at saying *dog* and bad at saying *which pixels*. The obvious repair — set the strides to one — fails for two reasons at once. Every subsequent filter's receptive field shrinks by the same factor, so the pretrained weights are now looking at a small fraction of the context they were trained on and their learned meaning is destroyed. And the maps balloon — dropping only the last two subsampling steps already makes them sixteen times larger in area, and removing all five a thousandfold — so both memory and computation become impractical. Resolution and receptive field appear to be the same dial.

They are not the same dial. A one-dimensional atrous convolution with rate $r$ is

$y[i] = \sum_{k} x[i + r\,k]\, w[k]$

which is the ordinary convolution at $r=1$ and, at larger $r$, samples the same $k$ weights from inputs spread $r$ apart. **The filter's footprint grows with $r$ while its parameter count and its output stride do not.**

The surgery follows directly. Set the stride of VGG's last pooling layers to $1$ and dilate every convolution after them by the compensating factor. Each filter then covers the same span of the image as before, the pretrained weights remain valid, no parameters are added, and the network's output stride is $8$. The trick is old — the algorithme à trous of undecimated wavelet transforms — but this is where it entered recognition.

blocks.h: Scale, by pyramid rather than by resizing
blocks.b: Objects appear at many sizes, and the usual answer was to run the whole network over an image pyramid and merge, which multiplies cost. Atrous spatial pyramid pooling instead branches at one layer into several parallel atrous convolutions with different rates — $6$, $12$, $18$ and $24$ in DeepLabv2 — and fuses their outputs. Each branch sees a different span of context using the same feature map and the same input pass, so multi-scale evidence costs a few extra filters rather than several forward passes. It is the direct analogue of an inception block for receptive field, and the idea recurs in PSPNet's pooling pyramid and in every DeepLab since.

blocks.h: The CRF, and why it was later removed
blocks.b:
Even at stride $8$ the predictions are smooth, and DeepLab's original answer was a fully connected CRF over pixels, with pairwise Gaussian potentials on position and colour, solved by a few iterations of mean-field inference. Pixels that are close and similarly coloured are pushed to agree, which snaps a label map to image edges and lifted results by a few points of mean IU; DeepLabv2 with a ResNet-101 backbone reached just under $80\%$ mean IU on PASCAL VOC 2012.

It was also a bolt-on: a non-differentiable post-process with hyperparameters cross-validated separately. CRF-as-RNN made the mean-field iterations trainable, and DeepLabv3 then dropped the CRF altogether once a batch-normalised ASPP and a stronger backbone made its contribution vanish. The stated need for structured post-processing turned out to be a symptom of a weak decoder.

Holding a stride-$8$ feature map through the deepest layers is expensive in memory and time, and it is why DeepLabv3+ eventually reintroduced a light decoder so the backbone could run at stride $16$. There is also a sampling pathology. A dilated filter reads a lattice, so with large rates adjacent output positions can be computed from disjoint sets of inputs — the gridding artefact — and as the rate approaches the size of the feature map, a $3\times3$ filter degenerates towards $1\times1$ because only its centre tap lands on valid features. Hybrid rate schedules and an image-level pooling branch were the responses.

Semantic Image Segmentation with Deep Convolutional Nets and Fully Connected CRFs

sam.lead: SAM reframed segmentation as a promptable task: given a point, a box or a rough mask, return a valid mask, whatever the object is and whether or not it has a name. Trained on a billion masks over eleven million licensed images — collected by a data engine in which the model annotated its own training set — it segments unfamiliar objects and domains zero-shot. What it does not do is say what anything is.

blocks.b:
Every strong segmentation model of the preceding decade was trained against a fixed class list: eighty things in COCO, a hundred and fifty in ADE20K, nineteen in Cityscapes. A model asked about anything outside its list has no representation of the question. Interactive segmentation existed separately — GrabCut and its deep successors would cut out whatever a user clicked — but each was a per-image tool, not a general prior over objects.

NLP had by then shown what the alternative looks like: a pretraining task general enough that downstream problems become prompts. Segmentation had neither such a task nor anything approaching the data scale, and the largest mask datasets were smaller than the image datasets by orders of magnitude.

The pretraining task is to return a valid mask for any prompt, where a prompt may be a foreground or background point, a box, a coarse mask, or text. Ambiguity is unavoidable and is designed for rather than around: a single click on a shirt might mean the shirt, the person, or a pocket.

SAM therefore emits **three masks per prompt, corresponding roughly to a subpart, a part and a whole**, and backpropagates only the loss of the best-matching one, so the outputs specialise instead of collapsing to their average. A separate head predicts each mask's IoU with the true object, which both ranks the candidates for a user interface and provides a confidence signal used later to filter automatically generated data.

blocks.h: A heavy encoder and a very light decoder
blocks.b:
The architecture is split by how often each part must run. An MAE-pretrained ViT-H processes the image once at $1024\times1024$ into a $64\times64$ embedding — the expensive step, and one that is amortised across every prompt on that image. The prompt encoder turns points and boxes into positional embeddings and text into a CLIP embedding.

The mask decoder is then only a couple of layers of two-way cross-attention, in which prompt tokens attend to the image embedding and the image embedding attends back, followed by an upsampling head. It runs in tens of milliseconds on a CPU in a browser, so a user's clicks are answered as they are made. Interactivity is an architectural constraint here, not a demo feature.

blocks.h: The data engine is the contribution
blocks.b:
SA-1B was built in three stages, each using the current model. First, annotators segmented interactively with SAM assisting and correcting; the model retrained on what they produced. Second, SAM pre-filled the masks it was confident about and annotators were asked only for what remained, which shifted effort towards rarer objects. Third, a regular grid of points was fed to the model automatically and its outputs filtered by predicted IoU and by stability under threshold perturbation.

The result — over a billion masks on eleven million licensed, privacy-protected images, the overwhelming majority produced automatically — is roughly two orders of magnitude more masks than any previous dataset, and it, rather than any component of the network, is what makes the zero-shot behaviour work.

SAM returns regions, not categories: it will happily segment an object it could not identify, which is the source of both its generality and its incompleteness. Practical use therefore pairs it with something that supplies labels, typically an open-vocabulary detector feeding boxes as prompts. Text prompting was demonstrated in the paper but was explicitly a proof of concept rather than a robust capability.

Quality gaps remained too: thin structures, wires and hair are missed or fragmented, and boundaries can be soft, which HQ-SAM addressed with a higher-resolution mask branch. The ViT-H encoder is too heavy for edge deployment, prompting MobileSAM and EfficientSAM, and SAM 2 later carried the same promptable formulation into video with a memory bank across frames.

vit.lead: ViT asked whether convolution's built-in assumptions about images are necessary or merely convenient, and answered by deleting them. An image is cut into fixed $16\times16$ patches, each linearly projected into a token, and the resulting sequence goes into a standard Transformer encoder with nothing image-specific added. Trained on enough data it beats the best convolutional networks; trained on ImageNet alone it loses — and that conditional is the finding.

blocks.b:
A convolutional network is not a generic function approximator applied to pixels. It hard-codes locality, in that early units see only a small neighbourhood; translation equivariance, in that weights are shared across positions; and hierarchy, in that resolution falls as semantics rise. These are excellent assumptions about photographs and they are why CNNs learn from modest datasets.

They are also constraints. By 2020 several works had tried to relax them — attention layers inserted into ResNets, ResNet stages replaced with local self-attention, sparse attention patterns over pixels — but these either kept the convolutional skeleton or required custom kernels to be efficient. What nobody had run was that control experiment at scale: Cordonnier et al. had already applied full self-attention to $2\times2$ patches, but no one had taken a Transformer unchanged from language, fed it large patches of ordinary images, and pretrained it on hundreds of millions of them.

An $H\times W$ image is cut into $N = HW/P^2$ non-overlapping patches of side $P$, each flattened and projected by a single matrix $E$. A learnable class token is prepended and learnable position embeddings are added:

$z_0 = [\,x_{\mathrm{class}};\; x_p^1 E;\; \dots;\; x_p^N E\,] + E_{\mathrm{pos}}$

The rest is the Transformer encoder verbatim — multi-head self-attention and MLP blocks with residual connections and layer normalisation — and a linear head on the final class token. At $224\times224$ with $P=16$ that is $196$ tokens.

The only image-specific decisions left are the patch size and the position embedding, and even the latter is weak: two-dimensional position embeddings performed no better than one-dimensional ones, since the model recovers the spatial arrangement regardless.

On ImageNet-1k alone, ViT trails a comparable ResNet by a few points. Pretrained on ImageNet-21k it draws level. Pretrained on the $300$-million-image JFT it moves ahead, with ViT-H/14 reaching $88.55\%$ top-1 on ImageNet at less pretraining compute than the convolutional baselines it displaces.

The paper's reading is the interesting part. **An inductive bias is a substitute for data.** Where examples are scarce, the CNN's assumptions supply constraints the data cannot, and it wins; where examples are plentiful, the same assumptions exclude solutions the data would otherwise support, and it loses. The crossing point sat somewhere around a hundred million images — which put the result out of reach of anyone without a proprietary dataset.

blocks.h: What was really doing the work
blocks.b:
Analysis of attention distances shows that some heads in the earliest blocks attend almost globally while others stay tightly local, so the model reconstructs something like a convolutional receptive field where that is useful and abandons it where it is not.

The stronger claim — that attention is intrinsically the better image operator — did not survive scrutiny. ViT arrived with a modern training recipe: AdamW, heavy augmentation and regularisation, long schedules, large batches. When ResNets were retrained under comparable recipes, and when ConvNeXt modernised a convolutional design point by point, most of the reported gap closed. The durable lesson concerns scale and training procedure at least as much as it concerns self-attention.

Three problems were handed to successors. Attention is quadratic in the number of patches, so high-resolution inputs are punishing and the patch size cannot simply be reduced. The representation is single-scale and non-hierarchical, which detection and segmentation heads expect otherwise — Swin and PVT reintroduced a pyramid, and ViTDet later argued a plain backbone suffices with the right adapter. And the data requirement was a barrier in itself, answered first by DeiT's augmentation and distillation, then more decisively by self-supervised pretraining in MAE, BEiT and DINO, which found the signal in unlabelled images instead. A minor practical wart persists: changing resolution requires interpolating the position embeddings.

refs.t: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale

deit.lead: DeiT showed that ViT's appetite for three hundred million images was a property of how it had been trained, not of attention itself. A carefully assembled regularisation and augmentation recipe brings a vision Transformer to competitive ImageNet accuracy using ImageNet alone, on a single eight-GPU machine in about three days; a distillation token, supervised by a convolutional teacher through self-attention, adds another point and a half.

blocks.h: A result with a precondition most labs could not meet
blocks.b:
ViT's headline claim came attached to JFT-300M, a proprietary dataset. That made the finding hard to build on and hard to check, and it left the causal question open: is a Transformer's data hunger intrinsic — the price of discarding convolutional priors — or an artefact of a training procedure inherited from language, where the regularisation needs are different?

The question mattered practically. If intrinsic, vision Transformers were a tool for organisations with private web-scale data. If procedural, they were available to everyone. DeiT's contribution is to settle it in the second direction, and to do so with a recipe published in enough detail to reproduce.

DeiT trains for $300$ epochs with AdamW, a learning rate scaled to batch size, stochastic depth, label smoothing, and a stack of augmentations: RandAugment, Mixup, CutMix, random erasing, and repeated augmentation, which draws several augmented copies of the same image within a batch. Fine-tuning at higher resolution follows.

DeiT-B, architecturally identical to ViT-B, reaches $81.8\%$ top-1 on ImageNet-1k using no external data. The ablation is as informative as the headline: removing almost any single component costs accuracy, and repeated augmentation in particular is needed for the long schedule to help rather than overfit. **Transformers are far more sensitive to the training recipe than convolutional networks are**, which is precisely why the original comparison was misread.

On top of the recipe, DeiT adds one architectural element: a learnable distillation token appended to the patch sequence beside the class token. It passes through every self-attention layer, interacting with patches and with the class token, and its output is supervised by the teacher's prediction while the class token is supervised by the ground-truth label. At test time the two predictions are averaged.

The point of putting distillation in a token rather than only in the output loss is that the teacher's signal shapes the internal representation, competing for attention with the label objective throughout the depth of the network. The two tokens do not collapse into one another: their outputs become increasingly similar in deeper layers, but remain measurably distinct and predict differently often enough to make averaging worthwhile.

blocks.h: Hard labels, and a convolutional teacher
blocks.b:
Two empirical choices look wrong and are not. First, hard distillation beats the usual soft KL objective here:

$\mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\psi(Z_s), y) + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\psi(Z_s), y_t), \quad y_t = \arg\max_c Z_t(c)$

where $Z_s$ and $Z_t$ are student and teacher logits and $\psi$ the softmax. Part of the explanation is the augmentation: a heavy crop or a Mixup can leave the recorded label describing something no longer in the image, whereas the teacher labels what the student is actually looking at.

Second, a RegNet convolutional teacher outperforms a Transformer teacher of equal accuracy. The student appears to inherit the teacher's inductive bias through its decisions — the convolutional prior arrives as supervision rather than as architecture. Distilled DeiT-B reaches $83.4\%$, and $85.2\%$ after fine-tuning at $384$.

The dependence on data is reduced, not removed; it is traded for a dependence on a strong pretrained teacher and an extra training run, and the student's ceiling is entangled with the teacher's quality and its errors. Nothing here explains how to train the first good model in a domain with no teacher available.

The more general answer came from self-supervised pretraining — MAE, BEiT and DINO — which extracts the necessary signal from unlabelled images and needs no teacher at all. DeiT III later revisited the supervised recipe with better augmentation and a simpler objective and recovered much of the distilled model's accuracy without distillation, which suggests the token was in part compensating for a recipe that was still improvable.
