mbv3.lead: MobileNetV3 is less a new architecture than the output of a pipeline: a platform-aware block search, a per-layer filter trim against measured latency, and a handful of hand-made corrections to the parts search could not see. Its durable contributions are cheap ones — hard-swish, a cheaper hard-sigmoid squeeze-and-excite gate fixed at a quarter of the expansion width (the SE-in-inverted-bottleneck block itself came from MnasNet), and a head redesigned by deleting work rather than optimising it.

blocks.h: What the search left on the table
blocks.b:
MnasNet had established that measured latency belongs in the reward, but a block-level search reasons about repeated structures and is blind to the two ends of the network, where a handful of layers carry disproportionate cost. MobileNetV3 runs the MnasNet search for the block layout, then applies NetAdapt to trim filter counts layer by layer against latency measurements, then fixes the ends by hand.

The final $1{\times}1$ expansion to the classifier width was moved to sit after the global average pool, so it runs on a $1{\times}1$ map rather than a $7{\times}7$ one; the bottleneck feeding it then became redundant and was removed outright. The stem's first convolution dropped from 32 filters to 16. Together these recovered roughly a tenth of total runtime at no cost in accuracy — pure bookkeeping the searcher had no way to find.

Swish, $x\,\sigma(x)$, had been reported to beat ReLU in deeper networks, but the sigmoid needs an exponential: expensive in fixed-point mobile runtimes and awkward to quantise. MobileNetV3 substitutes a piecewise-linear surrogate,

$$h(x) = x\,\frac{\mathrm{ReLU6}(x+3)}{6}$$

which tracks swish closely enough to preserve accuracy while compiling to a clamp, an add and a multiply, and quantises without a lookup table. The same treatment is applied to the sigmoid gate inside squeeze-and-excite.

Both are used selectively rather than everywhere. **The cost of a pointwise nonlinearity scales with feature-map area**, so hard-swish appears only in the second half of the network where the maps are small and the accuracy gain is nearly free; SE blocks appear only in some stages, with the bottleneck fixed at a quarter of the expansion width so the extra parameters stay contained.

blocks.h: Two models rather than one multiplier
blocks.b: The family ships as Large and Small, each searched against its own latency target, rather than one network shrunk by a width multiplier — the point being that a good architecture at 200 milliseconds is not a scaled copy of a good architecture at 20. Large reaches just over 75% top-1 on ImageNet, roughly three points above MobileNetV2 at meaningfully lower latency on a Pixel phone; Small serves budgets where V2 was already stretched thin. A companion segmentation head, LR-ASPP, strips the atrous spatial pyramid down to a global-pooling branch and a $1{\times}1$ path. The result became the default mobile backbone for several years; EfficientNet, published within weeks of it, inherited the same squeeze-and-excite inverted bottlenecks from their shared MnasNet ancestor and kept full swish, while its Lite variants dropped SE and swish altogether for the sake of quantisation.

Every choice here is conditioned on one target: a particular ARM CPU running TFLite. A mobile GPU, DSP or NPU orders the same candidates differently, so a network searched for one is not optimal on another, and retargeting means rerunning the search — which is precisely what the weight-sharing supernets, once-for-all among them, were built to avoid.

The deeper limitation is arithmetic intensity. Depthwise convolutions cut multiply-adds without cutting memory traffic, so they leave wide accelerators idle and their nominal savings do not convert into wall-clock savings on hardware built for dense matrix products. Later designs partly reversed course: EfficientNetV2 replaced early depthwise blocks with fused ones, and GPU-targeted families went back to plain convolutions that look wasteful on paper and run faster in practice.

refs.t: Searching for MobileNetV3
MnasNet: Platform-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Mobile

nasnet.lead: NASNet made architecture search useful by shrinking what gets searched. Rather than a whole network, a controller searches two small cells on CIFAR-10; the cells are then stacked to whatever depth and width the target task wants. It was the first demonstration that a motif discovered on a cheap proxy task transfers to a dataset the search never saw.

blocks.h: The cost of searching a whole network
blocks.b:
The 2017 predecessor had a controller RNN emit an entire architecture layer by layer, trained by policy gradient on its children's validation accuracy. It worked on CIFAR-10 and did not scale. The description length grows with depth, so a deeper network is a longer and harder sequence to sample; and the result is welded to the resolution and label set it was searched at, so nothing carries over to ImageNet, where the compute would actually have been worth spending. Searching directly on ImageNet was out of the question at the time.

NASNet's premise is an observation about the hand-designed networks it was competing with. Inception and ResNet are a repeated module plus a stacking rule. **Search should produce the module and leave the stacking to the practitioner** — which makes the search space independent of the final network's size.

Two cells are searched: a Normal Cell that preserves feature-map size and a Reduction Cell that halves it with stride two. Each is assembled from five blocks. For every block the controller emits two inputs, chosen from the cell's own inputs and the outputs of earlier blocks; an operation for each, drawn from a fixed menu of separable convolutions from $3{\times}3$ to $7{\times}7$, pooling, identity and dilated convolution; and a combiner, either addition or concatenation. Block outputs nothing else consumes are concatenated to form the cell's output.

Because every decision is a choice among discrete options with tensor shapes fixed by construction, every sample is a valid, trainable network — no repair step, no invalid children. The controller was trained with proximal policy optimisation, and ScheduledDropPath, dropping paths at a rate that rises through training, proved necessary to regularise the discovered cells.

Stacking the discovered cells produced NASNet-A at several sizes, controlled by how many times the Normal Cell repeats and how wide it is. The large model reached 82.7% top-1 on ImageNet, ahead of the best published results of the day, and a mobile-scale variant beat hand-designed networks at comparable multiply-adds. The learned features also carried into detection: substituting the backbone into Faster R-CNN gained around four points of COCO mAP.

The numbers mattered less than what they licensed. A cell found on $32{\times}32$ images, judged by briefly-trained children, was competitive at $331{\times}331$ after full training. Every subsequent search method rests on that proxy assumption, and NASNet is where it was first shown to hold.

blocks.h: The bill, and the later verdict
blocks.b:
A single search cost on the order of two thousand GPU-days — reproducible by a handful of laboratories and nobody else. Two lines of work followed. One attacked the cost: ENAS shared weights across children, and DARTS relaxed the discrete choice into a differentiable mixture, finishing in about a day.

The other attacked the claim. Random sampling within the same cell space turned out to be a strong baseline, which suggests much of the gain came from the hand-designed space rather than the controller searching it. The cells are also awkward in deployment: many small fragmented parallel branches keep multiply-adds low while occupying a GPU badly, so latency does not follow the FLOP count. MnasNet's response was to stop counting and start measuring.

refs.t: Learning Transferable Architectures for Scalable Image Recognition
Neural Architecture Search with Reinforcement Learning

mnasnet.lead: MnasNet is where architecture search stopped optimising a proxy and started optimising the quantity actually wanted. Candidate networks are executed on a real phone, their measured inference latency enters the reward directly, and the search space is loosened so that different stages of the network may take different structure.

blocks.b:
Earlier searches either maximised accuracy alone and squeezed the winner afterwards, or used multiply-adds and parameter counts as a stand-in for speed. The proxy fails in a documented and specific way: MobileNetV1 and the mobile NASNet sit at nearly identical multiply-add counts — roughly 570M each — and still differ by more than half in measured latency on the same handset. Depthwise convolutions, fragmented parallel branches and memory traffic are priced quite differently by a real runtime than by an arithmetic count, and the discrepancy is not a constant factor that cancels out of a comparison.

Any analytic surrogate would also have to be re-derived for each device, each inference engine and each quantisation setting. **Running the candidate on the target hardware removes the modelling problem rather than improving the model** — at the price of one more engineering loop inside the search.

blocks.h: A reward shaped like the Pareto front
blocks.b:
The objective is a scalarisation with a deliberate shape:

$$\max_{m}\ \mathrm{ACC}(m)\left[\frac{\mathrm{LAT}(m)}{T}\right]^{w}$$

where $T$ is the latency target and $w$ the trade-off exponent. A hard constraint — full reward inside the budget, penalty outside — returns only models sitting at $T$ and discards everything the search learned about neighbouring budgets. Setting $w \approx -0.07$ instead makes the reward approximately flat along the accuracy–latency frontier. The value is calibrated against an empirical regularity: doubling latency tends to buy about five per cent relative accuracy, so weighting the ratio by that slope gives models across a range of speeds comparable reward, and a single search returns a usable family rather than a single point.

A NASNet-style search returns one cell repeated everywhere, forcing every stage of the network to share a structure. MnasNet instead partitions the network into a fixed number of blocks and searches each independently: convolution type (regular, depthwise separable, or inverted bottleneck with an expansion ratio), kernel size three or five, squeeze-and-excite ratio, skip connection type, output filter count, and how many identical layers the block repeats.

Holding layers within a block identical is what keeps the space tractable — its size is roughly the per-block option count raised to the number of blocks, not to the number of layers. The discovered models mix $3{\times}3$ and $5{\times}5$ kernels across depth in ways no repeated cell can express, and the ablation attributes real latency savings to that irregularity.

MnasNet-A1 reaches roughly 75% top-1 on ImageNet at about 78 milliseconds on a Pixel — considerably faster than MobileNetV2 at higher accuracy, and faster still relative to the mobile NASNet. Its blocks are the direct ancestor of MobileNetV3, which adds NetAdapt trimming and hand-corrected stem and head, and of EfficientNet-B0, found by the same search with FLOPs substituted for latency because no single device was being targeted.

What did not improve was accessibility. The search trains thousands of candidates on a proxy task and stays out of reach for most groups, and its answer is valid for one device, one runtime and one numeric format. Retargeting means re-searching, which is the problem once-for-all and the weight-sharing supernets were built to eliminate.

refs.t: MnasNet: Platform-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Mobile

efficientnet.lead: EfficientNet's claim is that the three ways of enlarging a convolutional network — depth, width and input resolution — are not independent knobs, and that raising all three together in a fixed ratio dominates raising any one. A small searched baseline scaled by that rule produced a family that held the accuracy-per-FLOP frontier on ImageNet for years.

blocks.b:
Before this, enlarging a network meant picking a dimension by taste. ResNet went from 18 layers to 200, WideResNet multiplied channels, other work simply raised the input size. The paper's empirical finding is that each dimension saturates on its own well before the compute budget is exhausted, and — the part that matters — that the saturation point of one moves when the others change.

The reason is not mysterious. A higher-resolution input contains finer detail; representing it needs more channels, and covering it needs more layers to build a receptive field that still spans the image. Scale resolution without depth and the deepest units never see enough context. Scale width without resolution and the extra capacity has nothing new to encode. The dimensions are coupled, so they should be set jointly.

One coefficient $\phi$ governs the budget; three constants fix how it is spent:

$$d = \alpha^{\phi},\quad w = \beta^{\phi},\quad r = \gamma^{\phi},\qquad \alpha\beta^{2}\gamma^{2} \approx 2$$

Here $d$, $w$ and $r$ multiply the baseline's depth, channel width and input side length. The constraint encodes how each dimension costs: doubling depth doubles multiply-adds, whereas doubling width or resolution quadruples them, so fixing $\alpha\beta^{2}\gamma^{2}$ at about $2$ makes total FLOPs grow as roughly $2^{\phi}$ and turns $\phi$ into a plain compute dial.

A small grid search on the baseline gives $\alpha = 1.2$, $\beta = 1.1$, $\gamma = 1.15$, and these are then frozen. B1 through B7 are the same three constants at increasing $\phi$, never re-searched — the search cost is paid once, at the smallest scale.

Compound scaling amplifies whatever it is applied to, so the starting network matters as much as the rule. EfficientNet-B0 was found by a MnasNet-style multi-objective search with FLOPs rather than measured latency in the reward, since no particular device was being targeted; it is a stack of inverted-bottleneck blocks with squeeze-and-excite, close in spirit to MnasNet itself.

B0 reaches about 77% top-1 with 5.3 million parameters. At the other end, B7 reaches 84.3%, matching the best published accuracy of the time with roughly an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Applying the same rule to ResNet and MobileNet improved them as well, which is the paper's real evidence: the gain belongs to the scaling law and not only to the block it was demonstrated on.

The frontier is drawn in FLOPs, and FLOPs are not time. Large members train slowly, exhaust memory at high resolution and force small batches; depthwise convolutions in the early, high-resolution stages barely occupy a modern accelerator; and scaling every stage by a common factor over-grows parts of the network that were already cheap. EfficientNetV2 addressed all three, with fused convolution blocks early, non-uniform stage-wise scaling under a cap on training image size, and progressive resizing with regularisation raised alongside it.

The comparison also flattered the architecture. A substantial share of the reported gain came from the training recipe — heavy augmentation, long schedules — and later work retraining ResNet-50 with the same modern ingredients closed much of the apparent gap.

refs.t: EfficientNet: Rethinking Model Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks
EfficientNetV2: Smaller Models and Faster Training

rcnn.lead: R-CNN put a convolutional network into object detection by not asking the network to do detection. An off-the-shelf proposal algorithm suggests some two thousand boxes per image, each is cropped, warped to a fixed size and classified by a network pre-trained on ImageNet. PASCAL VOC mAP, which had been creeping up a point a year, moved by twenty.

blocks.b:
VOC detection was dominated by deformable part models over HOG features, dressed up with ensembles and context rescoring, and the numbers had plateaued in the low thirties. Meanwhile AlexNet had just shown that a learned feature hierarchy beat hand-designed features on ImageNet classification by an unarguable margin.

Two obstacles kept the result from crossing over. The first is localisation: a classifier says what, not where, and the dense sliding window that worked for a cheap HOG template is impractical over a deep network with a large receptive field and a coarse stride. The second is data. Detection annotation was scarce — VOC offers a few thousand labelled images with boxes — and a network with tens of millions of parameters cannot be fitted to that from a random initialisation.

Selective Search produces category-independent proposals by hierarchically grouping superpixels: about two thousand boxes with high recall of true objects at any scale, for a fraction of the cost of exhaustive search. Each is dilated slightly, warped anisotropically to $227{\times}227$ — aspect ratio deliberately not preserved, which ablations found better than padding — and pushed through AlexNet.

The answer to scarce data is the part that outlived the architecture: **supervised pre-training on ILSVRC classification, then fine-tuning on detection**, counting proposals above $0.5$ IoU with a ground-truth box as positives. The 4096-dimensional penultimate activations then feed one linear SVM per class, greedy non-maximum suppression removes duplicates, and a class-specific ridge regression on mid-level features nudges each surviving box, worth several points of mAP.

53.3% mAP on VOC 2012, more than thirty per cent relative above the previous best, and the same features scored 31.4% mAP on the ILSVRC2013 detection set after the competition had closed — well clear of the 24.3% reached by the sliding-window OverFeat system and of the 22.6% that had won the track. A gap that large in a mature benchmark ended the argument about whether learned features belonged in detection.

Two secondary findings had as much influence. Pre-train-then-fine-tune became the default response to any vision problem with too little labelled data, for a decade. And layer-wise ablation showed that most of the representational value sits in the convolutional stack rather than the fully-connected head — removing the last two dense layers barely hurt — which is the argument for treating a classification network as a general-purpose feature extractor at all.

The pipeline recomputes everything. Two thousand heavily overlapping crops each get their own full forward pass, so inference runs to tens of seconds per image and training caches hundreds of gigabytes of features to disk.

It is also three systems bolted together. The network, the SVMs and the box regressors are trained separately, with different definitions of a positive example, so nothing is optimised against the final metric; and the proposals come from a fixed hand-designed algorithm sitting entirely outside the learning. SPPnet soon showed the convolutional work could be shared across proposals, but could not propagate gradients below its pooling layer, leaving the backbone frozen. Fast R-CNN lifted that restriction and folded classifier and regressor back into a single network with a single loss.

Spatial Pyramid Pooling in Deep Convolutional Networks for Visual Recognition

fastrcnn.lead: Fast R-CNN turns detection back into one network trained with one loss. The image is convolved once, every proposal pools its own fixed-size feature from the shared map, and classification and box regression are learned jointly. It trains roughly nine times faster than R-CNN, runs over two hundred times faster at test time, and is more accurate than either R-CNN or SPPnet.

blocks.h: What SPPnet got right, and wrong
blocks.b:
The waste in R-CNN is obvious once stated: overlapping proposals recompute identical convolutions. SPPnet fixed the test-time half by computing the feature map once for the whole image and spatial-pyramid-pooling each proposal's sub-window into a fixed-length vector, worth one to two orders of magnitude.

Its training stayed R-CNN's: extract features, write them to disk, fit SVMs, fit box regressors afterwards. Worse, fine-tuning could not update any layer beneath the pooling operation. With each mini-batch RoI drawn from a different image, the backward pass through the pyramid was hopelessly inefficient, so the convolutional stack stayed frozen at its ImageNet weights — capping accuracy exactly where a deep network has most to contribute.

RoI pooling is single-level spatial pyramid pooling: a region of size $h \times w$ on the feature map is divided into an $H \times W$ grid of roughly $h/H$ by $w/W$ cells, and each cell is max-pooled, yielding a fixed $7 \times 7$ feature for any region shape. Max pooling has a well-defined subgradient — each input location accumulates gradient from every RoI whose bin selected it — so error flows straight into the shared convolutions.

What makes that affordable is the sampling. A mini-batch takes two images and 64 RoIs from each, rather than 128 RoIs from 128 images, so all RoIs from one image share a single forward and backward pass through the backbone: a roughly sixty-fold saving. The feared correlation between same-image samples did not impede convergence.

Two sibling outputs sit on the pooled feature: a softmax over $K+1$ classes and per-class box offsets, trained together as

$$L = L_{\mathrm{cls}}(p,u) + \lambda\,[u \ge 1]\,L_{\mathrm{loc}}(t^{u}, v)$$

where $L_{\mathrm{cls}} = -\log p_u$ is the log loss for true class $u$, the indicator switches localisation off for background regions, and $L_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is a smooth $L_1$ — quadratic near zero, linear beyond — so badly predicted boxes cannot produce the exploding gradients that a plain squared error does under a shared learning rate.

Joint training beat staged training, and the softmax slightly beat the SVMs it replaced, retiring R-CNN's most awkward component. Truncated SVD on the dense layers cut another third from test time, the per-RoI head having become the bottleneck once convolutions were shared.

blocks.h: The proposals were now the problem
blocks.b:
With a VGG-16 backbone, detection takes about 0.3 seconds per image excluding proposals, while Selective Search takes roughly two seconds on a CPU. **The learned part of the system had become an order of magnitude cheaper than the hand-engineered stage in front of it**, and no further optimisation inside the network could change the total. That arithmetic is the entire motivation for Faster R-CNN, which generates proposals from the same shared feature map.

Two other seams remained. RoI pooling quantises region coordinates twice, once onto the feature grid and once into bins, misaligning features from pixels — corrected later by RoIAlign. And duplicate suppression is still a greedy NMS threshold chosen by hand, outside the loss entirely.

fasterrcnn.lead: Faster R-CNN notices that the convolutional features computed to classify regions are already enough to propose them, and hangs a small proposal network off the same shared map. Proposals become nearly free, the detector becomes a single network, and the anchor box introduced here became the standard vocabulary of object detection for the next five years.

blocks.h: A two-second bottleneck in front of a 0.3-second network
blocks.b:
Fast R-CNN had made the learned part of detection cheap enough that Selective Search dominated the clock: roughly two seconds per image on a CPU against 0.3 seconds for the network. Reimplementing the proposal algorithm on a GPU was the obvious response and the wrong one. Hierarchical superpixel grouping ports badly, and porting it would leave the real defect untouched.

That defect is that proposals were hand-designed, tuned once on one dataset, and entirely outside the learning. Nothing the detector found difficult could feed back into what it was shown, and the recall ceiling of the proposal stage silently capped the accuracy of everything downstream. If the features can classify a region, they ought to be able to say whether the region is worth classifying.

blocks.h: Anchors and the region proposal network
blocks.b:
A $3{\times}3$ convolution slides over the shared feature map; at each position two $1{\times}1$ convolutions predict, for each of $k = 9$ anchors — three scales crossed with three aspect ratios, centred there — an objectness score and four coordinate offsets.

Anchors are what let one feature map at one scale cover objects of many shapes. Rather than resizing the image into a pyramid or the filters into a pyramid, the reference boxes are enumerated, and the $k$ regressors do not share weights, so each specialises to one shape and only has to predict a small residual. Anchors above $0.7$ IoU with a ground-truth box are positive, below $0.3$ negative, the rest ignored; the loss is Fast R-CNN's — log loss on objectness plus smooth $L_1$ on offsets parameterised relative to the anchor.

blocks.h: Making the backbone do both jobs
blocks.b:
The saving comes entirely from sharing. Because the RPN reads the same convolutional map the detector uses, proposals cost on the order of ten milliseconds rather than two seconds. Arranging that sharing was originally a four-step alternating schedule: train the RPN from an ImageNet initialisation, train Fast R-CNN on its proposals, re-initialise the RPN from the detector's tuned convolutions with those layers now frozen, then fine-tune only the detector's own layers. The same paper showed approximate joint training — treating proposal coordinates as constants in the backward pass, and simply dropping the gradient with respect to the boxes — works nearly as well, trains appreciably faster and is far simpler.

Three hundred learned proposals then suffice where Selective Search needed two thousand, and accuracy rose rather than fell: 73.2% mAP on VOC 2007 with VGG-16, at about five frames per second including proposals.

The pipeline is still two-stage with a per-RoI head, so cost grows with proposal count, and several components sit outside the objective. Anchor scales and aspect ratios are hyperparameters needing re-tuning per dataset. Foreground–background imbalance is managed by sampling a fixed ratio of negatives rather than by the loss, a heuristic that focal loss later replaced. Duplicate removal remains greedy NMS with a hand-picked threshold. And a single-scale feature map serves small objects poorly, which FPN addressed by pooling each RoI from an appropriate pyramid level.

The following decade removed each in turn: anchor-free dense predictors dropped the reference boxes, and DETR recast detection as set prediction with Hungarian matching, deleting anchors and non-maximum suppression together.

refs.t: Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks

wrn.lead: Wide ResNet asked whether the thousand-layer headline of the residual-network papers was where the accuracy actually came from. Widening each residual block by a factor $k$ and cutting depth back to a few dozen layers matched the deepest thin models at comparable parameter counts, and trained several times faster on the same hardware.

blocks.b:
Identity shortcuts made very deep training possible, and the follow-up work pushed to 1001 layers on CIFAR. The returns were thin: an order of magnitude more depth bought a fraction of a percent, at a training cost that made the models impractical to iterate on.

Zagoruyko and Komodakis pinned the cause on **diminishing feature reuse**, a failure mode named in the earlier work on highway networks and stochastic depth. When every block is wrapped in an identity path, nothing forces any particular block to do work — gradient descent is free to leave a block close to the identity and route the signal past it. A very deep thin stack therefore ends up with many blocks contributing almost nothing, and depth is buying capacity in a form the optimiser can decline to use.

The change is one number. A WRN-$n$-$k$ keeps ResNet's three stages and its two-$3\times3$ block, but multiplies every stage's channel count by $k$: the usual $16, 32, 64$ become $16k, 32k, 64k$. WRN-28-10 — 28 layers, ten times the width — was the workhorse configuration, and a 16-layer wide network reached the accuracy of a 1000-layer thin one at a similar parameter count.

Widening adds parameters faster than deepening does, so the model needs regularisation the thin networks did not. The paper puts dropout between the two convolutions inside each block, on the residual branch rather than the identity path, and shows it helps consistently once the width is up.

blocks.h: Why wide is faster at equal work
blocks.b:
The wall-clock gain is not a FLOP saving; it is a utilisation one. A thin deep network is a long chain of small matrix products with a strict sequential dependency, and each one leaves most of a GPU idle. A wide shallow network does the same total arithmetic in fewer, much larger products, which is the shape the hardware is built for.

The result also sat well with the emerging reading of residual networks as implicit ensembles of many short paths rather than one very deep function. If the effective computation is shallow anyway, spending the budget on depth is spending it on something the network does not use, and width is the honest way to buy capacity.

Width is not free either. Parameters grow roughly with $k^2$ and activation memory linearly with $k$, so at a fixed accuracy a wide model is a large file and a heavy training footprint, and the CIFAR result did not transfer wholesale to ImageNet, where depth kept earning more of its place. The paper also gives no principle for choosing $k$ and $n$ together — both came out of a sweep.

That is the gap EfficientNet closed, by making depth, width and input resolution a single compound scaling rule under a fixed budget, and RegNet by treating the whole design space statistically rather than sampling points in it. Dropout inside the block, meanwhile, was largely displaced by stochastic depth and heavier augmentation.

refs.t: Wide Residual Networks

densenet.lead: DenseNet connects every layer to every later layer within a block and passes features forward by concatenation rather than addition. Because nothing is summed away, each layer needs to contribute only a handful of new channels — a growth rate of 12 or 32 — while still seeing everything computed before it, which is why it reached ResNet-level ImageNet accuracy with roughly half the parameters and half the computation.

blocks.h: A sum is a lossy join
blocks.b:
A residual block computes $x_\ell = H_\ell(x_{\ell-1}) + x_{\ell-1}$. The identity term guarantees a gradient path, which was the point, but the addition is destructive: the two summands are gone, and a later layer that wants the early feature on its own cannot have it. Any reuse of an early representation has to survive being repeatedly overwritten by additions along the way.

DenseNet keeps them apart instead:

$x_\ell = H_\ell\big([x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{\ell-1}]\big)$

where $[\cdot]$ is channel concatenation. Every earlier feature map remains individually addressable at every later layer, so **reuse is a matter of reading rather than of preservation**. A block of $L$ layers has $L(L+1)/2$ connections rather than $L$.

$H_\ell$ is batch norm, ReLU and a $3\times3$ convolution producing exactly $k$ channels — the growth rate, typically 12, 24 or 32. Layer $\ell$ therefore sees $k_0 + k(\ell-1)$ input channels: the input widens linearly with depth while each layer's own output stays narrow.

Two economies keep that affordable. The bottleneck variant puts a $1\times1$ convolution producing $4k$ channels in front of each $3\times3$, so the expensive convolution never sees the full accumulated width. Concatenation also requires a fixed spatial size, so the network is split into dense blocks joined by transition layers — batch norm, $1\times1$ convolution, average pooling — which halve the resolution and, with compression $\theta = 0.5$, halve the channel count as well.

Parameter efficiency was the clearest gain: a DenseNet matched the ImageNet error of a ResNet with about half the parameters, because it never re-learns a feature it could have read. The margin was largest on CIFAR without augmentation, which points at a regularising effect — with the collective state shared, individual layers have less to memorise.

There is a second, structural benefit. Every layer has a short path both to the input and to the loss through the classifier's access to the concatenated stack, which acts as implicit deep supervision of the kind auxiliary heads were bolted on to provide. Inspecting the learned weights showed late layers genuinely reading early feature maps, so the reuse was real rather than nominal.

The naive implementation is quadratic in activation memory: each layer allocates a fresh contiguous copy of the concatenation plus its own normalised output, and none of it can be freed until backward. Pleiss and colleagues fixed this with shared storage and recomputation of the concatenation and batch norm in the backward pass, bringing memory back to roughly linear for a modest increase in time — but the fix is an engineering trick, not a property of the architecture.

Throughput lagged too: many small convolutions and constant concatenation are memory-bandwidth bound, so measured speed fell short of the FLOP count. CSPNet went at exactly that, splitting a stage's feature map so only half passes through the dense block, which cut both duplicated gradient information and cost.

Memory-Efficient Implementation of DenseNets

resnext.lead: ResNeXt replaces a residual block's single wide transformation with $C$ parallel transformations of identical topology, summed. That count — cardinality — is offered as a third scaling axis beside depth and width, and under a fixed parameter and FLOP budget, spending on it beat spending on either of the others.

blocks.h: Inception's split-transform-merge, minus the hand design
blocks.b:
Inception had already shown that a block of several differently shaped branches, concatenated, is cheaper than one dense convolution of equal expressive reach. The cost was that every branch carried its own filter sizes, widths and pooling choices, tuned stage by stage; adapting the design to a new dataset or a new compute budget meant redoing that work.

VGG and ResNet had the opposite virtue — one block repeated, so an architecture is a couple of numbers. ResNeXt takes Inception's strategy and imposes ResNet's uniformity on it: **all branches have the same topology, so the module gains one hyperparameter rather than a dozen**. Nothing about the branches has to be designed; only how many of them there are.

The block computes

$y = x + \sum_{i=1}^{C} \mathcal{T}_i(x)$

where each $\mathcal{T}_i$ is the familiar $1\times1$ reduce to width $d$, $3\times3$, $1\times1$ expand. Three forms of this are exactly equal in arithmetic: $C$ separate branches summed; a single $1\times1$ reduction whose output is split, transformed and concatenated before one $1\times1$; or, most usefully, a plain bottleneck block whose $3\times3$ is a grouped convolution with $C$ groups. The last is what ships, because it is one kernel call.

Capacity is held fixed by trading $C$ against $d$: ResNeXt-50 in its $32\times4d$ form runs 32 paths of width 4 and has essentially ResNet-50's parameters and FLOPs.

The experiment that matters holds complexity constant and moves capacity between the axes. Doubling $C$ while halving $d$ improved ImageNet top-1 consistently, and improved it more than making the same block deeper or wider would have. At larger scale a 101-layer ResNeXt bettered a 200-layer ResNet at about half the computation, and the architecture took second place in the ILSVRC 2016 classification task.

The interpretation the paper offers is that grouping constrains the block usefully. A dense $3\times3$ over all channels can express any mixing, but the optimiser does not find a better solution in that larger space; forcing the transformation into independent subspaces is a prior that pays, rather than a restriction that costs.

blocks.h: Cheap in FLOPs, less so in time
blocks.b:
Grouped convolution has poor arithmetic intensity — many small independent matrix products, each moving as much memory as it does work — so measured throughput lags the operation count, and at the time the library kernels for grouped convolution were not well optimised. A model can be strictly cheaper on paper and no faster on the device.

Cardinality also remains a number set by sweep rather than derived, which is the same complaint ResNeXt made of Inception, one level up. RegNet later searched a parametrised design space and found group width a genuinely useful axis, giving the choice an empirical basis; ResNeSt kept the groups and added attention across the splits. Taken to its extreme, $C$ equal to the channel count is depthwise convolution.

refs.t: Aggregated Residual Transformations for Deep Neural Networks

senet.lead: Squeeze-and-Excitation adds a global, per-channel gate to a block that already exists: pool each feature map to a single number, push the resulting vector through a small bottleneck, and rescale every channel by the sigmoid that comes out. It costs well under a percent in FLOPs, transfers to any backbone unchanged, and won ILSVRC 2017 with a top-5 error of 2.251%.

blocks.h: Channel mixing is stuck at the receptive field
blocks.b:
A convolutional filter fuses spatial and channel information at once, within its window. That means a layer's judgement about which channels matter is made locally and is entangled with local spatial structure — in early layers, from a patch a few pixels across.

But whether a texture channel or a colour channel is informative is often a property of the whole image, not of any patch in it. The architecture as it stood had no cheap route for that information: a global judgement requires a receptive field the size of the input, which in a plain convolutional stack only arrives near the end. Most of the work on this seam had gone after the spatial axis — multi-scale branches, dilation, attention over positions. SENet goes after the other one.

Squeeze is global average pooling, one scalar per channel:

$z_c = \frac{1}{HW}\sum_{i=1}^{H}\sum_{j=1}^{W} u_c(i,j)$

Excitation is a two-layer gate on that vector, $s = \sigma\big(W_2\,\delta(W_1 z)\big)$, with $\delta$ a ReLU, $W_1$ reducing the width by $r = 16$ and $W_2$ restoring it. The output channel is scaled: $\tilde u_c = s_c u_c$.

Two choices carry the design. The reduction $r$ keeps the parameter cost down and, more importantly, forces the gate to model relationships between channels rather than store a value for each. And the non-linearity is a **sigmoid, not a softmax** — the channels are not competing for a fixed budget of attention, so several can be emphasised at once.

blocks.h: Nearly free, and it moved everywhere
blocks.b:
The unit sits after the last convolution of a residual block, before the shortcut is added, which is what makes it a drop-in. SE-ResNet-50 lands within a whisker of ResNet-101's ImageNet accuracy while keeping ResNet-50's compute, at roughly ten percent more parameters — most of which sit in the final stage, where the channel count is largest and where removing the SE blocks costs very little.

Because the unit only touches channels, it composes with anything: SE-ResNeXt, SE-Inception, and later the mobile line, where MobileNetV3 and EfficientNet both carry it inside their inverted-residual blocks as standard equipment. Channel recalibration went from a paper to a default component in about two years.

SE has no spatial selectivity at all — it can say which channels matter but not where. CBAM added a spatial gate alongside the channel one, and the non-local and global-context blocks went after long-range spatial dependence directly.

The bottleneck was also challenged on its own terms: ECA-Net argued that the dimensionality reduction is harmful, since it forces channel relationships through an indirect low-rank map, and replaced the two fully connected layers with a single 1D convolution over neighbouring channels — fewer parameters, comparable or better accuracy. And global pooling is a synchronisation point: the entire feature map must exist before any part of it can be scaled, which complicates streaming inference and layer fusion on the very devices where the FLOP cost looked negligible.

ECA-Net: Efficient Channel Attention for Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

xception.lead: Xception takes the hypothesis implicit in every Inception module — that cross-channel correlation and spatial correlation can be learned separately — and pushes it to its limit, mapping channels with a $1\times1$ convolution and then filtering each resulting channel entirely on its own. The network is a stack of those depthwise separable convolutions with residual connections, and at Inception V3's parameter count it did better, most clearly on Google's internal 350-million-image dataset.

blocks.h: What an Inception module was assuming
blocks.b:
An ordinary convolution learns filters over a three-dimensional space — two spatial axes and the channel axis — jointly. An Inception module does not: it first projects the input through $1\times1$ convolutions into several smaller channel spaces, then applies $3\times3$ or $5\times5$ filters within each of them.

Chollet's contribution is partly to state the premise that made this work and had never been written down: **learning the channel factorisation and the spatial factorisation separately is easier than learning them together**. If that is true, the number of branches is an arbitrary point on a continuum, and the interesting question is what happens at the end of it — one independent spatial filter per output channel.

blocks.h: The extreme case is a familiar operator
blocks.b:
A $1\times1$ convolution over all input channels, followed by an independent $3\times3$ on each of its outputs, is a depthwise separable convolution with the two halves in the opposite order and — the difference that mattered — no activation function between them.

The ordering turns out to be immaterial once the blocks are stacked, since the boundary between one block and the next is arbitrary. The missing non-linearity was not. Inserting a ReLU between the pointwise and depthwise stages slowed convergence and lowered final accuracy, which is the opposite of what the same experiment shows inside an Inception module. Chollet's explanation is the depth of the intermediate space: a ReLU discards information from a one-channel feature map that it would not discard from a wide one.

blocks.h: The network, and what it demonstrated
blocks.b:
Thirty-six convolutional layers in fourteen modules, arranged as an entry flow, a middle flow repeated eight times and an exit flow, with linear residual connections around every module but the first and last. The residuals were not decoration — without them the same stack trained to a markedly worse result.

The parameter count matches Inception V3 almost exactly, which is what makes the comparison informative. The ImageNet gain is small; the gain on the much larger internal dataset, measured on FastEval14k — 14,000 densely annotated images spanning some 6,000 classes — is substantial. The reading is that separability does not add capacity but uses it better, and that the advantage grows with the amount of data available to fill that capacity.

Full separability is a modelling assumption, and it forecloses filters that are genuinely joint in space and channel. It holds well enough in practice, but nothing establishes it as more than a good approximation, and later work reintroduced partial coupling — mixed kernel sizes, or grouped rather than fully separated channels.

The other cost is arithmetic intensity. A depthwise convolution does very little work per weight and per byte moved, so it is memory-bandwidth bound and its measured throughput falls well short of its FLOP saving: Xception ran at roughly Inception V3's wall-clock speed despite a different operation mix. That gap is precisely why the primitive paid off first at the small end, in MobileNet, where memory traffic was the budget anyway.

refs.t: Xception: Deep Learning with Depthwise Separable Convolutions

mobilenet.lead: MobileNet is a network built entirely from depthwise separable convolutions, with two global knobs — a width multiplier and a resolution multiplier — that let one architecture be dialled to a device's budget rather than redesigned for it. At about a thirtieth of VGG-16's parameters it came within a point of its ImageNet top-1 accuracy.

blocks.b:
A standard convolution with $D_K \times D_K$ kernels mapping $M$ channels to $N$ over a $D_F \times D_F$ map costs $D_K^2 M N D_F^2$ multiply-adds, because it filters and combines in one operation. Splitting those two jobs gives one depthwise filter per input channel and then a $1\times1$ convolution to combine:

$D_K^2 M D_F^2 + M N D_F^2$

The ratio of the second to the first is

$\frac{1}{N} + \frac{1}{D_K^2}$

With $3\times3$ kernels and any realistic $N$, that is a factor of eight to nine saved for a small accuracy cost. Xception had used the same primitive to spend a large budget better; MobileNet uses it to make the budget small.

blocks.h: Fast on the hardware that existed
blocks.b:
The structure is a full convolution followed by thirteen separable blocks, each half getting its own batch norm and ReLU, then average pooling and a classifier. The detail that made it fast in practice is where the arithmetic lands: roughly 95% of the multiply-adds and three-quarters of the parameters sit in the $1\times1$ convolutions, which are a dense matrix product needing no `im2col` rearrangement and therefore run near the peak of the BLAS kernels phones actually had.

Training needed a corresponding adjustment. The depthwise filters carry very few parameters and underfit rather than overfit, so they are given little or no weight decay — regularisation tuned for a large model is the wrong setting for a small one.

The width multiplier $\alpha \in \{1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25\}$ thins every layer, reducing cost by roughly $\alpha^2$; the resolution multiplier takes the input from 224 down to 128 pixels, again quadratically. Together they define a family of models on a smooth accuracy-latency curve, so a deployment picks a point instead of commissioning an architecture.

The ablation behind this is the useful part. At matched compute, a thinner MobileNet beats a shallower one: removing layers costs more accuracy than narrowing all of them. Depth in this regime is doing real work, and the intuition that a small model should be a short model is wrong. That result shaped how the mobile line was scaled for years afterwards.

blocks.h: What it left for its successors
blocks.b:
Accuracy falls away sharply at the small end, and $\alpha$ and the resolution were chosen by sweeping, not derived — the paper offers a family, not a rule for picking from it. Two deeper problems went unnoticed until later. The block ends with a ReLU on its narrow output, which MobileNetV2 argued destroys information a thin layer cannot afford to lose. And cost was reported in multiply-adds, a proxy ShuffleNet V2 and MnasNet both showed can rank real devices wrongly, since memory access and kernel support matter as much as arithmetic.

The answer to the hand-tuning was search: MnasNet and MobileNetV3 optimised blocks against measured on-device latency, and EfficientNet turned the multipliers into a single compound scaling rule.

refs.t: MobileNets: Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks for Mobile Vision Applications

mbv2.lead: MobileNetV2 inverts the residual block: the shortcut now joins the thin bottleneck tensors, the expansion happens inside the block, and the projection back down is left linear. Both changes follow from one claim — that a ReLU applied to a low-dimensional tensor destroys information no later layer can recover — and together they reached higher ImageNet accuracy than v1 at roughly half the operations.

blocks.h: The ReLU at the narrow end
blocks.b:
MobileNetV1's block finishes with a $1\times1$ convolution that combines channels, followed by batch norm and a ReLU — and in a network already thinned by the width multiplier, that ReLU lands on a low-dimensional tensor. Sandler and colleagues argue that this is where accuracy was leaking. A ReLU preserves complete information about its input only on the region where it acts linearly; everything mapped to zero is collapsed irreversibly. If the features of interest occupy a manifold that only just fits in the narrow layer, a large share of it is destroyed.

Their demonstration is direct: embed a two-dimensional spiral into $n$ dimensions with a random matrix, apply a ReLU, project back. At $n = 2$ or $3$ the spiral is mangled beyond recognition; by $n = 15$ or $30$ it survives largely intact. Width is what buys a ReLU its reversibility.

The block takes a narrow tensor of $C$ channels, expands it with a $1\times1$ convolution by a factor $t$ (usually 6) with ReLU6, applies a $3\times3$ depthwise convolution with ReLU6, then projects back to a narrow output with a $1\times1$ convolution and **no non-linearity at all**. The residual connects the narrow tensors when the stride is one and the channel counts agree.

That inverts ResNet's bottleneck, which is wide at its ends and thin in the middle. The paper ablates both halves of the change: restoring a ReLU after the projection hurts, and moving the shortcut onto the expanded tensors instead of the bottlenecks is worse than leaving it where it is.

The tensors crossing block boundaries are now the small ones, and the large expanded tensor exists only inside a block. Because the depthwise convolution acts on each channel independently, that expansion can be computed and consumed a few channels at a time, so an inference engine need never materialise the full $tC$-channel tensor at once — peak memory is governed by the bottleneck sizes and the largest single block.

This matters more than the parameter count. On a phone or a microcontroller the binding constraint is fast on-chip memory holding activations, not the weights sitting in flash, and an architecture whose interfaces are narrow gives the runtime somewhere to put the intermediate work.

blocks.h: Results, and the search that followed
blocks.b:
At 3.4 million parameters and about 300 million multiply-adds the model reaches 72.0% ImageNet top-1, above v1 at roughly half its arithmetic. ReLU6 rather than ReLU is chosen for robustness under low-precision arithmetic, since a bounded activation quantises predictably. The block also carried over into detection as SSDLite and into segmentation as a DeepLabv3 backbone.

What remained hand-set was everything numerical: the expansion factor, the per-stage widths, the layer counts. MnasNet searched those against latency measured on an actual phone rather than against multiply-adds, and MobileNetV3 added squeeze-and-excitation and h-swish on top of that search. The inverted residual itself outlived its network — EfficientNet's MBConv is the same block.

maskrcnn.lead: Mask R-CNN adds a small fully-convolutional mask branch to Faster R-CNN and, in doing so, exposes a defect nobody had needed to care about: RoIPool quantises coordinates twice, and the resulting half-bin misalignment is invisible in a bounding box and fatal in a pixel mask. Replacing it with RoIAlign — bilinear sampling, no rounding — made instance segmentation a nearly free addition to detection.

blocks.b:
RoIPool maps a proposal in image coordinates onto a stride-16 feature map, rounds the boundary to integer cells, divides that region into a fixed grid of bins, and rounds again. Either rounding can displace the sampled region by up to half a feature-map cell — eight input pixels at stride 16, more at stride 32.

For classification, and for a box regressed against the RoI as a whole, this is tolerable: the head is asked for an answer that is invariant to exactly this kind of shift. A mask is a spatial output at feature resolution, so a shift in where the features were read is a shift in the mask itself. The quantisation was a defect the box task had been hiding.

RoIAlign drops every rounding. The RoI boundary stays in floating point, each bin is sampled at four regularly spaced points, and each sample is bilinearly interpolated from the four nearest features. The gain is largest where the stride is coarsest — on a stride-32 map the paper reports several points of mask AP over RoIPool, concentrated at high IoU thresholds, where alignment is what is being measured.

The mask branch is deliberately dull: a small FCN predicting a $28\times28$ binary mask **per class**, trained with per-pixel sigmoid and binary cross-entropy on the ground-truth class channel only. The decoupling matters. Earlier methods let classes compete through a softmax over the mask, which makes the mask argue about identity; here the classification branch decides what, and the mask branch only decides where.

blocks.h: A general head, not a segmenter
blocks.b:
The loss is $L = L_{\mathrm{cls}} + L_{\mathrm{box}} + L_{\mathrm{mask}}$, three parallel heads over the same aligned features, trained together. Nothing in the mask branch is specific to masks: swap the binary target for a one-hot map per keypoint and the same model does human pose estimation, which is how one architecture beat the COCO 2016 challenge winners on detection, instance segmentation and keypoints alike.

The mask branch adds only a small overhead over Faster R-CNN — the complete model still runs at about five frames per second. The practical claim — that instance segmentation is detection plus a cheap dense head, provided the features are read from the right place — is what made this the default segmentation baseline for years afterwards.

Twenty-eight by twenty-eight is a small canvas for an object filling most of the image, and upsampling it to the box gives visibly blocky boundaries on large instances; PointRend later recast mask prediction as adaptive point sampling to recover the edges.

Everything else came over from Faster R-CNN too: region proposals, IoU-threshold assignment, NMS, and the premise that every instance is a box first. Amorphous background regions have no box at all, so panoptic segmentation needed a second, differently shaped model alongside. Mask classification — DETR's set prediction generalised to masks in MaskFormer — eventually dissolved that split by predicting a set of labelled masks and letting one architecture cover objects and background alike.

detr.lead: DETR poses detection as direct set prediction: a transformer decoder emits a fixed number of outputs in parallel, a Hungarian matching assigns each ground-truth object to exactly one of them, and everything that existed to reconcile duplicates — anchors, IoU assignment rules, non-maximum suppression — is deleted rather than improved. It matched a well-tuned Faster R-CNN on COCO, and needed roughly an order of magnitude more training epochs to get there.

blocks.b:
Every detector before it predicted many overlapping candidates and then reconciled them. Anchors defined the candidate set, an IoU threshold decided which anchor was responsible for which object, and NMS deleted near-duplicates at inference. Each step is a heuristic with its own constants — anchor scales and ratios, positive and negative thresholds, an NMS cutoff — tuned per dataset and not differentiable.

The deeper problem is that the loss is defined on individual anchors, so the network is never told that two of its outputs describe the same object. It learns only, after the fact, that one of them will be discarded. **Duplicate suppression sat outside the objective it was meant to shape.**

DETR emits a fixed set of $N=100$ predictions and pads the ground truth with a no-object class $\varnothing$. Training first finds the permutation minimising total assignment cost,

$$\hat{\sigma} = \arg\min_{\sigma} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{match}}\big(y_i, \hat{y}_{\sigma(i)}\big)$$

where $y_i$ is a ground-truth object and $\hat{y}_{\sigma(i)}$ the prediction assigned to it. The Hungarian algorithm solves this exactly, and a class log-likelihood plus a box loss are then applied on that assignment.

Because the matching is one-to-one, a second prediction of the same object is penalised as a false positive by construction — precisely what NMS had been doing by hand. The box term mixes $\ell_1$ with generalised IoU, since $\ell_1$ error scales with box size and large objects would otherwise dominate.

A CNN backbone produces a feature map, flattened into a sequence with fixed positional encodings and passed through a transformer encoder — global self-attention over the whole image, whose attention maps visibly separate instances.

The decoder takes $N$ learned object queries, embeddings with no dependence on the input, and attends both among themselves and to the encoder output. Self-attention among the queries is what lets them coordinate: one query can see that another has already claimed an object. Trained queries specialise to rough regions and box-size regimes. The heads are a linear class projection and a three-layer MLP for the box, applied to every query in parallel, so inference is one forward pass with nothing after it but a confidence threshold.

The published schedule is 500 COCO epochs where a Faster R-CNN baseline uses tens. Two causes were identified afterwards: the matching is unstable early, so a query is assigned different objects between iterations and receives inconsistent targets; and cross-attention starts near-uniform over all spatial positions and must slowly learn to concentrate.

Small objects were the weak column, since a single stride-32 map carries them poorly and attention over finer maps is quadratic in their size. Deformable DETR answered both by attending to a few learned sampling offsets per query across scales, reaching comparable accuracy in a fraction of the epochs; DN-DETR and DINO stabilised matching with denoising queries. A mask head per query extended the same model to panoptic segmentation, the thread MaskFormer took up.

Deformable DETR: Deformable Transformers for End-to-End Object Detection

yolo.lead: YOLO discarded the propose-then-classify pipeline and made detection a single regression from image pixels to box coordinates and class probabilities, evaluated once per image. At 45 frames per second against Faster R-CNN's seven, it traded roughly ten points of mAP on PASCAL VOC for real time, and established one-stage detection as its own line rather than a cheap approximation of the two-stage one.

blocks.b:
R-CNN's descendants worked in stages: propose regions, extract features per region, classify, regress the box, suppress duplicates. Even Faster R-CNN, which folded proposal generation into the network, still ran its head hundreds of times per image and trained components against separate objectives. No single quantity being minimised corresponded to detection quality, and the repeated per-region work was where the time went.

YOLO's argument was that a proposal stage is a mechanism for deciding where to look, and a convolutional network that sees the whole image at once has already decided. Removing the stage removes both the duplicated computation and the seams between separately trained parts.

The image is divided into a $7\times7$ grid. Each cell predicts $B=2$ boxes — centre offsets within the cell, width and height relative to the image, and a confidence meant to equal $\Pr(\mathrm{Object}) \cdot \mathrm{IoU}$ — plus one set of $C=20$ conditional class probabilities shared by both boxes. The output is a single $7\times7\times30$ tensor from one pass of a 24-layer network.

Training uses sum-squared error, with two corrections that name the failure modes. Coordinate error is weighted by $\lambda_{\mathrm{coord}}=5$ and the confidence of empty cells by $\lambda_{\mathrm{noobj}}=0.5$, because most cells contain nothing and would otherwise drive all confidences to zero. Width and height are regressed in square roots, so a fixed absolute error counts for more in a small box than a large one.

Because the network conditions on the entire image rather than on a cropped region, it makes markedly fewer background false positives than Fast R-CNN — roughly half as many in the paper's error analysis. It also transfers better to artwork, where local texture changes but layout does not.

The two error profiles are complementary enough that the paper combines them, using YOLO to veto Fast R-CNN's background detections and raising the latter's VOC score in the process. That result is an early demonstration that a one-stage and a two-stage detector do not make the same mistakes, which is why the one-stage line was worth continuing even while it was behind on accuracy.

Localisation was the dominant error: boxes are regressed from scratch without anchors as a starting point, and the coarse grid leaves little spatial precision. The structural limit is harder. One class distribution and two boxes per cell caps how many objects a region can express, and two objects in the same cell cannot both be recovered — which is why flocks of birds and crowds were unreadable. Features come from a single heavily downsampled map, so small objects have little left to detect with.

SSD answered with default boxes across several feature maps, YOLOv2 adopted clustered anchors and higher resolution, and YOLOv3 added multi-scale prediction. The grid survived; being the only scale did not.

refs.t: You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection

ssd.lead: SSD kept YOLO's single forward pass but replaced its one coarse grid with default boxes tiled over six feature maps of decreasing resolution, so an object's scale is handled by which layer predicts it rather than by resizing anything. It reached Faster R-CNN's VOC accuracy at roughly ten times the speed, and made multi-scale prediction from one pass the standard shape of a one-stage detector.

blocks.b:
Detectors of 2015 handled scale in one of two expensive ways: run the network over an image pyramid, or predict from a single feature map and hope the regressor covers the range. YOLO took the second route, and its lone $7\times7$ map — receptive field tuned for medium objects — had little informative to say about small ones. Faster R-CNN's anchors gave several scales at one location, but all read from the same layer, so a small anchor and a large anchor shared a receptive field.

The observation SSD acted on is that a convolutional network already computes a scale pyramid internally: every stride reduction is another scale, and all but one of them was being discarded.

Predictions come from six maps of a VGG-16 base extended with extra convolutions, from $38\times38$ down to $1\times1$. At every location of every map a $3\times3$ convolution predicts, per default box, four offsets and $C+1$ class scores. Box scales are spaced roughly linearly across the layers from about $0.2$ to $0.9$ of the image side, with aspect ratios of $1$, $2$, $3$ and their reciprocals.

A default box is matched to an object when their overlap exceeds $0.5$, so several boxes may be responsible for one object — unlike YOLO's single accountable cell, which made the target sparse and the gradient scarce. Prediction is fully convolutional and shared across positions, so every scale costs one pass.

blocks.h: Two details that carried the result
blocks.b:
The ablations are more interesting than the architecture. The tiling yields thousands of candidates of which nearly all are background, so SSD sorts negatives by confidence loss and keeps only the worst, holding negatives to three times the positives — an explicit sampling heuristic that RetinaNet would later replace with a loss.

And **data augmentation is worth more mAP than any architectural choice in the paper**. Alongside random crops, a zoom-out operation pastes the image into a larger canvas of mean pixels, manufacturing small training objects that the dataset does not otherwise contain. The `conv4_3` predictions also need an explicit L2 normalisation, because that layer's activation scale differs from the deeper ones and the shared head cannot absorb both.

Small objects remained the weak column even so. The high-resolution maps that can see them are shallow: `conv4_3` has the spatial detail but not the semantics, having passed through too few layers to represent identity well. Predicting from each level independently leaves no path by which deep features can inform shallow ones.

FPN built exactly that path — a top-down pathway with lateral connections, so every pyramid level is both fine and semantically strong — and it is the FPN form of multi-scale prediction, not SSD's, that later detectors adopted. RetinaNet inherited SSD's dense default-box formulation on an FPN backbone and replaced the hard-negative mining with a reweighted loss.

Feature Pyramid Networks for Object Detection

retinanet.lead: RetinaNet's contribution is diagnostic before it is architectural: one-stage detectors trailed two-stage ones not because dense prediction is inferior, but because the summed loss over roughly a hundred thousand anchors is dominated by easy negatives. Focal loss reshapes cross-entropy to suppress that contribution, and with it a plain dense detector on an FPN backbone overtook every two-stage model of its year.

blocks.b:
A two-stage detector filters. The RPN cuts on the order of $10^5$ candidate locations to one or two thousand proposals, and the second stage samples those with a fixed positive-to-negative ratio or by hard-example mining, so its head sees a roughly balanced batch.

A one-stage detector has no such filter. It scores every anchor at every location of every pyramid level, and the handful containing an object are outnumbered by background by three or four orders of magnitude. Each easy negative contributes a small loss, but there are enough of them that their sum overwhelms the gradient from the rare positives. Sampling was the standard remedy, and RetinaNet's argument is that it is the wrong shape: it discards examples rather than reweighting them.

Write $p_t$ for the probability the model assigns to the correct class. Cross-entropy is $-\log p_t$; focal loss multiplies it by a modulating factor,

$$\mathrm{FL}(p_t) = -\alpha_t\,(1-p_t)^{\gamma}\log p_t$$

with $\gamma = 2$ and $\alpha = 0.25$ in the paper's setting. At $\gamma=2$ an example already classified at $p_t = 0.9$ has its loss cut by a factor of a hundred, while one at $p_t = 0.1$ is barely touched. Nothing is thrown away; the easy majority simply stops setting the agenda.

The $\alpha$ term supplies the residual class-frequency weighting, and its best value moves opposite to $\gamma$ — the modulating factor is already suppressing much of what $\alpha$ was introduced to suppress.

blocks.h: A detail without which it diverges
blocks.b:
Focal loss alone destabilises the first iterations, when every anchor sits near $p = 0.5$ and the summed background loss is enormous. RetinaNet initialises the bias of the final classification layer so that the prior foreground probability is about $0.01$, putting the model where it will spend the rest of training and making the first epoch survivable.

The remaining design is conventional and deliberately so: ResNet with FPN, nine anchors per location at three scales and three aspect ratios, and two small four-layer subnets for classification and box regression shared across pyramid levels. Keeping the architecture ordinary is the experimental point — the loss should be the only thing that varies.

The ablations make clear that the FPN backbone carries a substantial share of the accuracy, so focal loss is better read as what removed the one-stage penalty than as the whole result.

What survived untouched was the anchor: nine per location with hand-chosen scales and ratios, assigned to objects by IoU thresholds that themselves need tuning, on a grid dense enough that most computation goes to background however it is weighted. FCOS and CenterNet dropped anchors and predicted per pixel; ATSS then showed that the remaining gap between anchor-based and anchor-free detectors was almost entirely about how positives are assigned rather than about anchors as such. DETR removed the assignment question by making it a matching.

FCOS: Fully Convolutional One-Stage Object Detection

yolov3.lead: YOLOv3 is a short technical report rather than a paper, and its content is three changes: prediction at three scales through an upsampling pathway, a Darknet-53 backbone with residual connections, and independent logistic class scores in place of a softmax. It matched RetinaNet's accuracy at the loose IoU threshold of $0.5$ while running several times faster, and trailed it badly at strict thresholds — a trade the report is unusually candid about.

blocks.b:
YOLOv2 had already repaired the first version's worst structural limits: anchor boxes chosen by $k$-means over the training set rather than by hand, box centres constrained to their own cell by a sigmoid so that early training does not diverge, batch normalisation throughout, and a higher input resolution.

What it kept was prediction from a single feature map. One map means one effective scale, and the small-object recall YOLO had been criticised for stayed roughly where it was. The available move was the one FPN had just demonstrated on two-stage detectors: use the network's own resolution hierarchy rather than only its last level.

Predictions are taken from three maps: the deepest, and two more formed by upsampling that map and concatenating each with an earlier, finer layer of the backbone. The nine $k$-means anchor clusters are split three per scale, largest assigned to the coarsest map. Each scale emits the same tensor of box offsets, one objectness score and the class scores, so only the resolution changes.

Darknet-53 replaces the earlier backbone with residual blocks and no pooling — downsampling is done by strided convolution. It reaches ImageNet accuracy comparable to much deeper ResNets at considerably higher throughput, which is the whole point: for a real-time detector, the backbone's speed is the detector's speed.

Each class gets its own logistic score trained with binary cross-entropy, and objectness likewise. The reason is the data rather than a modelling preference. A softmax asserts that classes are mutually exclusive, and on datasets such as Open Images they are not — "Woman" and "Person" describe the same box, and forcing them to compete corrupts both.

Objectness is assigned to a single best-matching anchor per ground-truth box; other anchors that overlap heavily are ignored rather than penalised, so the loss does not punish a nearly correct prediction for losing the match. Later detectors converged on both choices for the same reasons, and label assignment became a research topic in its own right.

The report states plainly what its numbers say: at $\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ YOLOv3 is competitive with RetinaNet at a fraction of the inference time, and at $\mathrm{AP}_{75}$ it is well behind. Its boxes are found but loosely placed. It goes on to question whether COCO's average over IoU thresholds from $0.5$ to $0.95$ measures anything human annotators agree on — a complaint about the metric that the field largely declined to accept.

Small-object AP improved sharply with the three scales, while medium and large objects stayed the weak column relative to RetinaNet. Redmon later withdrew from computer-vision research over its military and surveillance applications, and the line continued under other authors, beginning with YOLOv4.

refs.t: YOLOv3: An Incremental Improvement

yolov4.lead: YOLOv4 is an engineering result presented as one: a controlled survey of training and inference techniques, assembled into a detector that trains on a single conventional GPU and runs above real time on one. Its new mechanisms are deliberately modest — mosaic augmentation, self-adversarial training, a cross mini-batch normalisation, tweaked SAM and PAN blocks — and it was the most useful detector of its year for anyone without a cluster.

blocks.b:
The stated target is a detector a practitioner can train on one 1080 Ti or 2080 Ti and deploy on one consumer GPU. That excludes most of what the accuracy leaderboard was doing — very large batches across many devices, backbones tuned for accelerator pods, multi-scale test-time ensembles — and it reframes the question. If the architecture must stay small and fast, the remaining levers are the ones that cost nothing at inference.

Hence the paper's organising distinction. A **bag of freebies** changes training only and leaves the deployed network byte-for-byte identical; a **bag of specials** accepts a small inference cost for a disproportionate gain. Almost every component already existed; what did not exist was a controlled account of which ones compose.

Mosaic augmentation stitches four training images into one, so each forward pass sees four contexts and objects appear at unusual scales against wrong backgrounds. Its side effect matters as much as its regularisation: batch-normalisation statistics are then computed over four images' worth of content, which is exactly what a small batch on a single GPU lacks.

Alongside it sit CutMix, DropBlock's structured spatial dropout, class label smoothing, cosine learning-rate decay, and CIoU loss, which adds centre-distance and aspect-ratio terms to IoU so that non-overlapping boxes still produce a useful gradient. Self-adversarial training perturbs the image against the network in one pass and trains on the result. None of it appears at inference time.

CSPDarknet-53 applies the cross-stage partial design: the feature map entering a block is split, one half passes through the dense computation, and the halves are concatenated after. Gradient information is not duplicated across the block's paths, cutting computation and memory for a small accuracy gain.

An SPP block pools at several kernel sizes to widen the receptive field without stride, and a PANet neck adds a bottom-up path to FPN's top-down one so that fine localisation signal reaches the deeper levels. Mish replaces Leaky ReLU in the backbone, and DIoU-NMS uses centre distance as well as overlap when suppressing, which helps in crowds. The assembly reaches the low forties in COCO AP at real-time speed on a V100.

Nothing here explains why the combination works. The ablations are largely one-at-a-time on a moving baseline, and several components plausibly do the same job twice. The detector also remains anchor-based, with IoU assignment and NMS at inference — all the machinery DETR was deleting in the same year.

What followed split the difference. YOLOX brought an anchor-free head with decoupled classification and regression branches; YOLOv5 shipped as engineering with no paper and a contested name; the same authors continued with YOLOv7's re-parameterised layers. The method YOLOv4 established — measure everything, publish the table, keep only what pays at inference — is what the line has done ever since.

refs.t: YOLOv4: Optimal Speed and Accuracy of Object Detection
CSPNet: A New Backbone that can Enhance Learning Capability of CNN

sam2.lead: SAM 2 folds image and video segmentation into one model by treating an image as a video one frame long, and gives that model a memory. Prompt an object on any frame with a click, a box or a mask and the segmentation is propagated through the clip, correctable later by another click wherever it goes wrong. On still images it is both more accurate than SAM on SAM's own zero-shot suite and about six times faster.

blocks.h: Per-frame masks are not a track
blocks.b: SAM segmented anything in a still image and nothing across time. Run frame by frame it produced masks with no identity: nothing tied a region in frame 40 to the same object in frame 41, so masks flickered, swapped between lookalikes, and needed an external tracker to reconcile them. Video object segmentation had the opposite shape: it took a full mask on the first frame, propagated it, and offered no way to correct a drifting track short of starting again. Two interfaces, and neither had the click-and-refine loop that made SAM usable.

The encoder is Hiera, an MAE-pretrained hierarchical ViT supplying multiscale features to the decoder's upsampling path. Between it and the mask decoder sits **memory attention**: the current frame's embedding cross-attends to a bank holding encoded features from a bounded number of recent frames, a bounded number of prompted frames, and object pointer vectors read off each frame's mask output token. Each entry fuses the downsampled predicted mask with that frame's embedding, so stored appearance is conditioned on the segmentation. Recent entries carry a temporal position encoding, so short-term motion is representable; prompted ones deliberately do not, since prompts are sparse in training and can arrive at inference from temporal ranges the model never saw. Frames stream in one at a time and the bank is FIFO, so memory stays bounded at any clip length.

In an image the object is present by construction; in video it leaves frame, passes behind something and returns. SAM 2 predicts an explicit occlusion score beside each mask, so a frame without the object yields no mask rather than a confident mask of the wrong thing. SAM's ambiguity machinery survives — several masks per prompt, ranked by a predicted-IoU head — but only the top-ranked one propagates, since carrying branching hypotheses through a stream is unaffordable. Training mirrors that loop: short sampled sequences, a couple of prompted frames, corrective clicks where propagation has gone wrong.

blocks.h: The data engine, a second time
blocks.b: SA-V was built as SA-1B was, the model annotating data for its own successor in three phases: SAM clicked frame by frame, then SAM 2 propagating from a mask, then full SAM 2 with click refinement. Annotation ran roughly eight times faster by the last phase, which put the scale in reach — over fifty thousand videos and some 35.5 million masks, well past the existing video benchmarks on both counts. Interface and dataset are one contribution: a promptable task lets annotation be model-assisted, and that assistance supplies the data the task needs.

A FIFO of recent frames is a short horizon. Through a long occlusion those entries fill with frames that do not contain the object, and the track drifts or reattaches to a lookalike; crowded scenes and large viewpoint changes fail the same way, and thin, fast-moving parts are lost. Objects are tracked independently too: the frame embedding is shared, but masklets never talk, so the model cannot use the fact that two of them cannot own the same pixel. And it still returns a region, never a name; the vocabulary was left to the concept-prompted successor.
